An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that seek to explain the behavior of $B^0_s$ time fluctuations. Furthermore, uncertainty arising from trigger mechanisms and unaccounted particle motion has been assessed, resulting in a range of 1.4 to 6.0 picobarns effectiveness.

This research paper focuses on a specific stochastic control problem, where the variable we aim to manage influences both the system's dynamics and how it experiences random fluctuations, similar to the work by J. Li and R. W. Brockett in 1998. We establish the existence of an solution to this problem based on the fact that the system's differential equation has solution existence, as well as the non-negative nature of the difference between the solution and a given target function. A strategy to find a minimizing sequence in the control set is proposed, which involves constructing the sequence based on a set of compact operators and applying the Berdundi - Opheim theorem. Additionally, a set of pointwise estimates is used to demonstrate that the set of candidate controls is compact in the set of allowable controls.

Our comprehensive study examined the anisotropy of very high-energy (VHE) cosmic rays using the HAWC observatory data from 2016 to 2020, which corresponds to energies beyond the Galactic disk and is influenced by the Local Bubble. We combined the HAWC data with that of the Fermi-LAB gamma-ray telescope to create an anisotropy map in the VHE energy range. The anisotropy was calculated using the differential flux, acceptance, live time, and the all-sky map of gamma-ray sources from the Fermi-LAB. The anisotropy was expressed as the excess probability, which indicated the likelihood of a source's emission contributing to the detected cosmic ray flux. The results revealed dipole-like modulations of 1.8 sigma at energies above 8 EeV and quadrupole-like modulations of 2.2 sigma at energies above 25 EeV. The expected contributions from giant molecular clouds and the Local Bubble were compared with our findings, and the data were also analyzed in relation to the VHE energy anisotropy reported by the LHC.
This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable.

This study presents first data on proton-lead collisions, specifically those with a center of mass energy of 5.72 TeV, and focuses on the analysis of Alice OCF flow angle and magnitude fluctuations, as seen from charged hadron distributions over wide angular ranges, both in overall angle $\Psi_s$ and local angle $\gamma$ relative to the largest asymmetric axis. These findings are drawn from low multiplicity data, encompassing between 20 and 100 GeV, and are contrasted with those from more symmetric collisions. Both scenarios exhibit fluctuation patterns, in both magnitude and angle, that are dependent on multiplicity and show little to no transverse momentum variation. They are linked to geometric fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions and are used to assess thermal models. In particular, the magnitude fluctuations in both cases are well described by the $1/N_{ch}$ pattern, in line with expectations from thermal models.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies within data tables, particularly when quality constraints are expressed as logical statements. These statements can be unsatisfiable, leading to the identification of data subsets that adhere to them. A key aspect of this work is accounting for inconsistencies in subsets of columns, ensuring robust solutions even when parts of the selected columns exhibit inconsistencies. This approach differs from traditional subset selection methods, which often assume subsetting includes removing rows with issues. Moreover, this method considers various data quality metrics, such as missing values and uncertain information. A logic-based framework is presented to address these concerns, utilizing a customized variant of the closed-world assumption. This framework is implemented in a prototype tool, with results demonstrated through an example.

This study introduces a novel dynamic econometric model (TVH-Poisson) that incorporates time-varying parameters and a flexible Poisson distribution with additional random variations, to enhance the accuracy of count time series forecasts. The TVH-Pisson model is particularly suitable for capturing complex dynamics in data that exhibit both deterministic and stochastic time variations. To efficiently estimate the model parameters and forecast future values, we developed an effective estimation algorithm using the EM approach combined with a numerical optimization method. Our results, based on simulated and real-world data, demonstrate that the TVH-Pisson model outperforms traditional Poisson and negative binomial models in improving forecast accuracy. The simulated data was generated using R, and the analyses were conducted using Python.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a new framework for object manipulation using hands. NDFs leverages a network of position-based neural descriptors to represent an object, which can then be queried to predict outcomes of actions. Unlike previous methods that aim to predict actions which lead to specific goal states, our approach focuses on predicting outcomes of actions to provide a causal model of the physical world. Crucially, we develop a causal descriptor that is invariant to rotations and translations in 3D space (a property known as SO(3)xR3-invariance), enabling predictions of actions that action the object to a new state, and a hand-grasping an object to a new state. We demonstrate a hand-grasping an object to achieve various task-related goals in simulation and a real-world setting.

Using the functional renormalization group approach, we have analyzed the phase transition point for the second-order transition in the universal phase of the Kosterlitz-Thouless type for the $N=2$ and $N>2$ O(N) universality classes. By calculating the effective action at the infrared cutoff, we have determined physical quantities such as thermal radii and complex singularities associated with a phase transition. Notably, we have found that the ratio of the residue of a complex singularity to the thermal radius converges to a fixed value for each universality class. Specifically, the value of this ratio, $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$, has been calculated as approximately 4.1 for $N=2$ and approximately 3.9 for $N>2$ universality classes, where $R_\chi$ is the thermal radius and $z_c$ is the characteristic distance of a complex singularity from the real axis.

In statistics and machine learning, estimating parameters often involves minimizing a non-convex risk function based on data samples. Researchers are particularly interested in understanding the local geometry of such optimization landscapes to develop more efficient estimation algorithms and gain insights into their behavior. This paper presents a significant breakthrough by establishing a strong local convexity property for empirical landscapes, which holds true in high-dimensional settings and is independent of condition number. The empirical convexity coefficient improves as the sample size increases, while the condition number-related coefficient increases with the dimensionality of the data. These findings lead to multiple convex geometry results for common iterative algorithms, including a tree-structured relationship among them. The development of a continuous function that describes the changing shape of the empirical landscape as a regularization parameter is also facilitated by these breakthroughs. This function allows for a comprehensive understanding of the changing critical points and Hessian eigenvalues of various optimization algorithms' landscapes as they respond to increased sample sizes.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmospheric particle composition is effectively demonstrated, achieving high precision is limited for applications requiring AOD measurements of 0.1 or less. To overcome this challenge, we developed a new technique for calculating the vertical AOD for sets of filter photometric passbands, minimizing the impact of systematic errors and random noise from photometric data. Our method, applied to the V-band data from the TESS mission, utilizes vertical and rutted AOD models to determine AOD underpasses that minimize AEP under the stars' light curves. Although initially designed for TESS data, this approach is versatile and can be used with any set of photometric filters and all-sky particle composition data. Our analysis reveals that for an ideal error-free dataset, the global average particle composition can be precisely determined to within 1.5% in a year, with a required sky coverage of 10^-5 per day. Although this coverage level is hypothetical, our study provides a framework for assessing particle composition precision using space-based all-sky photometry, with a view towards more precise measurements using instruments like TESS.

Recently, deep learning has become a key component in developing algorithms to estimate the 6D orientation of objects in images. Existing approaches can be broadly divided into two groups: those that rely on large databases of example data and those that use model-based methods without such extensive datasets. Although numerous studies have been conducted in this field, comprehensive comparisons have been limited. This study conducts a thorough review of the current state of the art, conducting detailed comparisons across multiple aspects of various methods in this field. This study systematically compares both traditional methods and deep learning-based approaches by analyzing their reliance on large datasets, handling of object symmetries, and performance on deformable objects. This study provides a robust platform for future researchers in this field to reference and build upon.

We present GGLasso, a Python library that combines Graphical Lasso and Sparse Group Lasso estimators based on scikit-learn. 
Initially based on the 'sgd' library, GGLasso utilizes a loop of Graphical Lasso and Sparse Group Lasso to solve the problem of covariance selection. 
It is an approximate solution that can be customized with different sparsity inducing norms and learning algorithms. 
Additionally, GGLasso includes a function to evaluate the stability of selected graph edges.

Numerous numerical techniques for solving partial differential equations have been successfully applied to calculate thermodynamic properties of biomolecules, including DNA and proteins, in solution. This has been particularly useful in determining how these molecules interact with each other and with drugs. This paper explores several of these methods, focusing on their ability to accurately determine the thermal motion and orientation of biomolecules. We examine the underlying assumptions of popular approaches, such as the use of Brownian dynamics to model the movement of DNA and proteins in solution, and we discuss the limitations and potential improvements of these methods. We discuss the potential limitations of current numerical methods, such as the use of finite difference methods to solve partial differential equations, and we discuss the potential benefits of using more accurate methods, such as spectral methods, to calculate the thermal motion and orientation of biomolecules in solution. Ultimately, we believe that by accurately calculating the configuration of biomolecules in solution, we can gain a deeper understanding of how these molecules interact with each other and with drugs, which has important implications for the development of new treatments for diseases.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. However, unlike the standard approach, our calculation takes into account the number of different layers a node appears in. We've developed the multi-layer eigenvector centrality framework by extending the standard concept, using the standard variation as a single-layer case, and developing a connection to the corresponding multi-layer adjacency matrix. Additionally, we've adapted the Nielsen and Kinchinel's infinite product definition from the complex domain to provide a rigorous definition of the corresponding multi-layer transition matrix.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock-Ivanenko brackets when applied to specific variables. 
This set of arrays constitutes the tangent space of a specific spacetime manifold, 
which corresponds to de Sitter spacetime when $R$ is infinite. A canonical Poisson 
bracket transformation is then shown to produce a modified version of the Paretic 
transformation, which also holds true for the quantum case. This finding suggests that 
$R$-Poincar\'e algebra can be understood as the low-energy, long-wavelength approximation 
of $R$-deformed Quantum de Sitter theory.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal, where a vapor cavity formed by the impact collapses and re-connects with the sphere's surface. Experiments were conducted using steel spheres ranging from 2.5 to 12.5 millimeters in diameter, dropped from heights between 0.1 and 2 meters into still water. High-speed imaging captured the seal formation process, with the time to seal, $t_s$, being compared to a characteristic time, $\tau$, derived from prior research. The results indicate that $t_s$ is directly proportional to $\tau$, but the proportionality factor changes with the ratio of the sphere's diameter to the impact site's vapor cavity radius, denoted as $\delta$. Specifically, for small $\delta$ values, the proportionality factor is approximately 4.2, whereas for larger $\delta$ values, it decreases to around 2.8.

A well-known phenomenon in physics is the quantization of generalized θ-terms, which are present in various effective field theories, including QCD, the axion-photon interaction, and the Chern-Simons term. These terms are closely linked to anomalies and topological properties, which pose a challenge to the study of quantum field theories from both the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian perspectives. In this research, a general proof is provided, demonstrating that generalized θ-terms, which appear in (d≥4)-dimensional theories and violate an n-form global symmetry, are inherently obstructed due to the cohomology of the symmetry. This general finding offers a new understanding of anomalies, including the case of the Chern-Simons term in d=3, and provides insights into the possible values of generalized θ-angles, such as those found in QCD and axion-photon interaction. This research has implications for the study of effective field theories, such as heavy quark effective theory and the Standard Model effective field theory.

We investigate the orbital-selective electron localization in cubanite, FeCu2S2, an antiferromagnetic semiconductor with a complex 3D spiral magnetic structure. Using density functional theory combined with dynamical mean field theory, we uncover that in cubanite, spatial and orbital polarization reinforce each other through a positive feedback mechanism. Initially, weak crystal-field splitting gives way to strong polarization driven by electron localization, which further amplifies itself. This phenomenon is also present in related compounds such as chalcocite and covellite but not in mackinawite, and it marks a distinguishing feature of FeCu2-based sulfides.

A significant portion of quantum dots with true spin-blockade dark excitons exhibit a longer radiative lifetime than bright excitons, making them highly desirable for creating long-lived coherent qubits. However, developing techniques to selectively address and manipulate dark excitons is challenging due to their significantly weaker interaction with light compared to bright excitons. We present a novel, wavelength-selective method to address dark excitons using a combination of a near-resonant laser pulse and an off-resonant two-photon pulse. By employing this technique, we experimentally observed a 60 percent reduction in the population of dark excitons, with potential applications in erasing, resetting, and reading out dark exciton states.

Researchers examined a two-dimensional electronic lattice from a stack of graphene sheets separated by dielectric material. By applying a specific pattern of electric currents between the layers, they achieved a unique arrangement of orbitals that results in isolated spins on each atom. Analysis revealed three key properties of this lattice: three distinct directions where the lattice is anisotropic, three different effective masses in perpendicular directions, and three separated Dirac points on electronic dispersion surfaces. A custom formula was developed to explain the extensive findings, which were experimentally validated using Raman spectroscopy and reported in multiple studies.

Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities of catalysis using these detection setups and derive the distribution of photons in the detected field. Furthermore, we analyze the nonclassical properties of the remaining field, finding that states resulting from beam splitter catalysis exhibit sub-Poissonian statistics and strong Sussman Gaussian squeezing, while those from the parametric amplifier catalysis display only weak squeezing. We also investigate the generation of SPCCSs in the far-field regime using a beam splitter, finding that the required detection conditions are more stringent in this case. Ultimately, our findings provide insight into the catalytic generation of single-photon states and the comparison between the two catalytic models.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles of the Newman-Penrose formalism when applied to a spherical symmetry scenario, specifically by exploring how to calculate the Newman-Penrose constants and determining the metric using the Weyl scalar method. As a result, the paper serves as a guide for converting any review or existing spherially symmetric solution into the full Newman-Penrose framework.

A recent study introduced a novel framework for designing chemical compounds using artificial neural networks, specifically for creating molecules with desired properties. This desired properties can take various forms, including numerical values, binary classifications, or even 3D molecular structures. The proposed method leverages a graph neural network to analyze the relationship between a molecule's structure and its properties, and employs an inverse modeling technique to generate candidate molecules through a generative process. This process involves a score-based model that gradually transforms random molecules into the desired structure, guided by neural operators that predict the desired properties. The framework ensures the discovery of diverse molecules with the target properties by incorporating a diversity term into its objective function. Researchers can easily incorporate new generative processes by defining the required dynamics. This framework has been successfully applied to four inverse modeling tasks, including predicting a molecule's structure based on its chemical composition and desired properties, and demonstrating its effectiveness through comparisons with existing methods.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be quite challenging for both humans and computers. The process of manually marking the tumors is also time-consuming and prone to errors. These difficulties are compounded by the varying sizes and shapes of tumors, their low contrast against surrounding tissue, and the presence of air or food within the esophagus that can obscure tumors. To tackle this problem, researchers have developed a deep learning-based method using 3D U-Net for segmenting tumors in the esophagus from CT scans. The method employs data augmentation techniques to increase the training dataset and improve the model's ability to detect tumors of different sizes and shapes. The results obtained using this approach are comparable to those of the state-of-the-art method known as DeepMedic.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective communication across linguistic barriers. When using multiple languages simultaneously, known as code-switching or code-mixing, the languages are interwoven at various levels, from entire sentences to individual words, letter combinations, or characters. Current state-of-the-art deep learning models for tasks like text classification and part-of-speech tagging rely on parallel multilingual texts, which are often unavailable for low-resource languages. To address this limitation, we explore the feasibility of training models for text classification and POS tagging using only monolingual resources across a spectrum of languages, from English to Lao. Our experiments with 12-layer RoBERTa models demonstrate that applying a WordPiece tokenizer and a linear classifier yields strong performance, achieving 80.59% accuracy for text classification and 90.35% precision for POS tagging on a 100-language setting. Furthermore, our models exhibit superior performance compared to the widely-used multilingual BERT models.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability is contingent upon the quality and diversity of these descriptions, the number of which can be prohibitively large. To address this issue, we present the 10 descriptions per image challenge, a proposal to replace the current standard and assess the potential benefits and drawbacks of this approach.

Recent research has focused on various tantalum oxide forms, including tantalum pentoxide, hydrated tantalum pentoxide, and oxide clusters, due to their interesting electrical and optical properties. Additionally, their biocompatibility and potential for drug delivery systems, combined with excellent capacity for anion adsorption, have made tantalum oxides of significant interest. In this work, we explore the structural and electronic properties of TaO$_x$ ($x$ = 1.5, 2, 2.5) using first-principles calculations. Our calculations reveal that all TaO$_x$ structures exhibit metallic behavior with a narrow band gap, and the Ta atoms in these structures display mixed oxidation states of Ta$^{5+}$ and Ta$^{4+}$. Furthermore, we find that the TaO$_x$ structures have a high work function, ranging from 5.48 to 5.9 eV, and display magnetic properties with a total magnetic moment of 1 $\mu_B$. Our results also suggest that TaO$_x$ could be effective in capturing anions, and its potential applications in high-performance transistors, optical devices, and even hadrontherapy for cancer treatment.

Individuals' non-cognitive characteristics, including their personality traits, are
likely to influence how they engage with and consume information online. This study
examines this link by analyzing data from over 45,000 Reddit users who consumed
news-related content from 2019 to 2021. Using a large-scale dataset of shared links,
comments, and user data from r/news and r/news_memes subreddits, in combination
with R. A. Baker Jr.'s (2021) Reddit User Open Personality (RUP) dataset, this study
investigates the impact of the personality trait of conscientiousness on the sharing
of news, including both accurate and false information across various political
ideologies and geographic locations. Our findings show that individuals with higher
conscientiousness are less inclined to share misinformation, particularly within
liberal news communities. This effect is more pronounced in politically moderate
and conservative areas. Furthermore, this influence varies across different
subreddits and is less pronounced in communities with a high level of news diversity.

Humans frequently learn new skills through observation, and this is also how robots typically acquire new skills.  However, programming complex robotic tasks remains a challenging and time-consuming process.  To address this, researchers have explored various methods for improving robot task learning, including using spoken instructions, demonstrations through code, physical actions, or even emotions.  Emotions expressed during a robot's action demonstrations can provide valuable information, yet there is limited knowledge on how to effectively utilize this information.  In this study, we investigate the possibility of using audio signals from human teachers during skill demonstrations to provide valuable prior knowledge for Robot Operation Prediction (ROP).  We categorize these audio signals into three key features: content, tone, and urgency.  By employing a multi-task learning approach, we trained a model to capture these features and found that urgency and tone provide meaningful information for both the prediction target and a secondary task.  Experimental results show that our approach, termed DARP (Demonstration w/Ah! prior), significantly outperforms traditional methods and even a baseline that leverages prior knowledge from action demonstrations alone.  Notably, we found that features representing tone and urgency are particularly beneficial, as they allow the prediction model to excel without increasing the number of prediction samples it needs to process.

Quantum computational complexity in 1+1 dimensional conformal field theories experiences a rapid increase over time both for its state and operator variants. Although the state and operator complexity growth has been previously observed in non-supersymmetric and supersymmetric models with non-trivial energy scales, this research delves into the behavior of complexity in conformal field theories, specifically focusing on Maxwell's action in the central charge limit. By employing the semi-classical approximation, we derive the time evolution of state and operator complexity for the conformal field theory, revealing that both complexities exhibit quadratic growth for a sufficient period before reaching a plateau. Notably, the rate of time evolution for state and operator complexity displays distinct characteristics, reflecting the inherent properties of the underlying theory.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, with many tech giants developing their own conversational agents. Although these agents excel at executing simple tasks, they struggle when it comes to understanding the broader context of a conversation. We investigate how to leverage past conversations to improve the comprehension of previous statements. By employing a self-supervised learning method, we enable past conversations to serve as valuable features in a conditional random field model. Our experimental results demonstrate that incorporating the conversation history can significantly enhance the interpretation of ambiguous statements, especially when a previous conversation is available. However, when a statement is unambiguous, past conversations do not provide substantial benefits. To incorporate the past conversation, we utilize a conditional neural sequence tagger as our baseline, and our experiments with this model show that our approach is both effective and efficient.

Cross-domain recommendation has gained significant attention in recent years, with numerous innovative approaches proposed to enhance the accuracy of recommendations. However, most existing single-to-single or multi-domain models concentrate on the primary domains, neglecting any sparse sub-domains. As a consequence, the effectiveness of cross-domain recommendations is compromised. In this study, we introduce a novel recommendation framework, called Multi-Sparse-Domain CoLiaborative RecCommenDation (MSDCR), which incorporates a sub-domain into the cross-domain recommendation process. Specifically, we leverage the rich data of dense domains and establish a coupled adversarial autoencoder (CAAE) to ensure that a target user's preference in a sparse domain remains compatible with the surrounding domain environment. To achieve this, we employ an CAAE to extract latent factors from user-item interactions across multiple domains, while a discriminative discriminator is designed to differentiate between the target and surrounding domains. Furthermore, we employ an auxiliary adversarial domain classifier to transform the target and surrounding domains to the same distribution. By leveraging these components, we optimize the CAAE to produce a surrounding domain that is more data-rich and beneficial for cross-domain recommendations. Our model is further improved by a collaborative feedback mechanism, allowing the target and surrounding domains to mutually benefit from each other. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over 14 state-of-the-art cross-domain recommendation baselines.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations, which underlie the driving force behind popular solvers like SDPT3, SEDuMi, and CIMPLEX. These tools gain their efficiency from exploiting exotic cones that are naturally incorporated into problems such as binary classification, manifold learning, and sparse recovery. In this research, we investigate the use of polynomial spline functions combined with a variety of exotic cones, including polyhedral, power, exponential, and Lorentz cones, to represent and solve regression, classification, and clustering problems. We also outline the practical applications of this approach in solving real-world problems such as image segmentation, sparse sampling, and count loss minimization, and provide code and data for a browser-based prototype of this code at http://www.exoticcones.com.

The rapid advancement of automated quality control methods in medical imaging, specifically MRI, has been facilitated by the development of various open-source tools and public datasets. However, with the increasing diversity of data available, it is crucial to understand how these algorithms perform across different populations. Our research re-evaluates the consistency of a state-of-the-art quality control framework, OC-RC, using 10 different datasets featuring MRI scans with artificial artifacts and clinical abnormalities. Our findings demonstrate that the algorithm effectively identifies various types of abnormalities and pathologies, although with differing levels of sensitivity. Additionally, our study reveals that the data set used to train the model significantly influences its performance, and that a more versatile training set can enhance its versatility. Ultimately, our research highlights the necessity of continuously monitoring and assessing the algorithm's performance across different populations to ensure reliable results.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical simulations were conducted to evaluate our method, which demonstrated significant improvements in solution quality and speed compared to traditional solvers.

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a recently introduced approach for managing multiple objectives in autonomous agents, has seen limited exploration of its application to mobile agents navigating complex environments while fulfilling multiple tasks. In a narrow setting that allows for an exact solution, we extend our research by comparing a refined variation of Motivation Dynamics to a revised hybrid method, which combines elements of action selection based on priority and regular Markov decision processes. Our findings are derived from a series of experiments using an agent tasked with navigating a grid to collect rewards while avoiding obstacles and walls, with the relative importance of these goals varying throughout the process. Our experiments involve a comparison between the proposed method and the hybrid approach, with results showing that the proposed motivation dynamics framework can efficiently handle situations where a agent must balance multiple, dynamically changing objectives, including scenarios with conflicting tasks and changing priorities.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3, and their respective lanthanide contraction series (LnSn3 with Ln = Dy, Tb, Ho, Er, Tm, Yb, Lu) in the A15 crystal structure. Our first-principles calculations show that all A15 LnSn3 compounds have a negative bulk modulus derivative, and GdSn3 and CmSn3 exhibit hexagonal close-packed (hcp) crystal structure. A comparison of A15 LnSn3 and A7 LnSn3 reveals that LnSn3 compounds in both crystal structures have similar electronic and magnetic properties. Notably, Sn 5s and 5p orbitals play a key role in the bonding of LnSn3 compounds, and the spin-orbit coupling effect is more pronounced in CmSn3 than in GdSn3. Furthermore, A15 LnSn3 exhibits a large negative magnetoresistance in a wide magnetic field range, and A15 GdSn3 displays a large magnetocaloric effect near its Curie temperature.

The paper discusses the challenges and constraints of a theoretical model known as the bilepton model, which extends the U(1) gauge group of the Standard Model. This model, which requires a significant change to the fundamental symmetry of particle interactions, has been shown to be inconsistent with experimental observations due to its prediction of a bilepton with extremely high mass and its interaction with a specific type of matter particle. To overcome these issues, researchers have explored alternative approaches, including changing the fundamental symmetry to a different value or introducing additional particles and forces. One such approach, based on an SO(N) symmetry, has been shown to be consistent with current experiments and may have important implications for our understanding of particle interactions and the evolution of the universe.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Gilula previously demonstrated that a RBS-based algorithm exists, capable of decomposing any Sn permutation into its OGS form. This research extends that RBS-based method to the broader class of finite classical Coxeter groups, known as Weyl groups, which includes both symmetric and bipartite permutations as subsets. As a result, a rationally expressible function describing the number of RBS representations with RBS bounds matching RGS bounds for a given magnitude is established for Weyl groups.

We've developed a method to calculate the changes in supernova magnitudes caused by the distribution of dark matter halos surrounding galaxies, using the NFW halo profile and existing models for supernova distributions. We focus on Type Ia supernoviae, which are more numerous and closer in distance compared to other types, making their bias easier to detect. Our calculations consider only line-of-sight effects, as transverse impacts are too complex to handle. We found that the lensing effects on supernovae are minimal and may be undetectable in certain cases, particularly for nearby supernoviae with certain types. We also discovered that the lensing-induced bias can be reduced if we use a combination of colours, but this requires a closer proximity to Earth and thus a smaller, more manageable dataset. We believe this approach could be used to test our assumptions and potentially provide evidence for superhalos surrounding galaxies.

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation of solid-state spin defects in materials that are transparent to specific wavelengths of light.  In silicon, T-type damage centers have shown great promise for creating high-quality photon-spin quantum interfaces, particularly when they undergo a process called the "zero-phonine hole transition" without any accompanying vibrations.  To take a significant step forward in using these damage centers for building quantum networks, we have used a scanning technique that rapidly maps out the relationship between specific physical locations and their corresponding resonance frequencies.  This technique allows us to identify the most suitable locations for applying small amounts of physical damage in order to create T-type damage centers with specific resonance frequencies.  By using this new technique, we have found large areas of silicon that can yield defect sites with very narrow line widths, allowing for precise manipulation of spin states through microwave radiation.

For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is necessary.
Different object detectors leverage scene information in various ways.
We categorize object detectors into three groups based on their context usage:
global, partial, and detailed.
The first group uses models that take inputs over the entire image,
such as those based on gradient mapping, and is represented by YOLOv4.
The second group involves models with partial inputs,
such as convolutional neural networks, and is exemplified by ResNet50.
The final group consists of models that process sequences,
such as convolutional neural networks, and is exemplified by SwinTransformer.
We compare the performance of these models in five different contexts:
color, rotation, scale, position, and shape,
by training and testing the object detectors on the CUB dataset.
We find that the YOLOv4 model's performance is limited in certain contexts,
particularly in handling partial inputs,
and that the ResNet50 model struggles with more complex inputs,
such as those with partial inputs,
and that the SwinTransformer model performs better in handling inputs with
partial inputs,
such as in the position context.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system that includes a small perturbation term. To achieve this, we leverage the combined method of homotopy and degree theory. Specifically, by applying these methods, we establish the existence of at least $2^{d-1}-1$ distinct solution pairs for system (1) under the given conditions.

We examine the behavior of tail probabilities for sums of random elements in the Grassmannian, selected according to the Yang–Lee measure. Assuming the underlying distribution is unimodal, we demonstrate that these tail probabilities follow a strong Stoyan order 2 pattern. For the specific case of the Yang–Lee measure defined on the Grassmannian with a deterministic element configuration, we establish two new integral inequalities of Hardy type for monotone functions of matrix variables. Moreover, these inequalities of Hardy type can be directly derived from the strong Rayleigh property exhibited by the Yang–Lee probability measure.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1961 work into English, which won the first prize at the International Mathematical Symposium in Newcastle upon Tyne for its significant contribution to the field.

A key obstacle in kidney transplants is the mismatch between available donors and patients in need of a compatible kidney. To overcome this challenge, researchers are exploring methods to make compatible transplants possible using incompatible kidneys. While this could significantly increase the pool of available kidneys, such transplants carry higher risks of rejection and complications, which could impact the long-term success of the implant. To minimize these risks and complications, it's crucial to have an ideal supply of rejection-medicine, known as antithymocyte globulin (ATG). However, ATG supplies are often insufficient, especially when performing multiple transplants simultaneously. To overcome this limitation, we introduce two mathematical models to determine the optimal usage of ATG for incompatible transplants, considering both immediate and long-term impacts on patient health. By applying these models to real-world data, we can identify strategies to balance the benefits of incompatible transplants with the available ATG supplies, ultimately improving the overall availability of compatible kidneys for patients.

This paper provides a detailed examination of the fundamental principles underlying NLP, with a specific focus on the use of neural embeddings. It begins by offering a comprehensive explanation of neural embeddings, then proceeds to explore the various types of embeddings currently in use. A thorough analysis of the underlying mechanisms of word embeddings is conducted, followed by a review of the embedding applications currently prevalent. A summary of the advantages and limitations of neural embeddings is also presented. A key aspect of the discussion is the demonstration of the intricate relationship between word embeddings and the distribution of terms within a given corpus, which is often overlooked in the existing literature. The paper also explores the current limitations of neural embeddings and presents the various alternatives that are available. It is hoped that the current survey will serve as a useful resource for both beginners and experts in the field of NLP, by providing a clear understanding of neural embeddings, their underlying mechanisms, and their current applications.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IEEE 802.11ad protocols as well as their physical layer features, modulation and error correction methods, OFDM signal generation, error management and subcarrier usage. It also explores the benefits and drawbacks of subcarrier usage, QPSK modulation, BCH error correction codes, TFC and TPC protocols, OFDM signal generation, MAC layer protocols, and security concerns related to the new wireless technology.

This research introduces a new method for modeling the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy using Cartesian grids to capture complex boundaries and solve the flow equations in a conservative manner. This strategy employs an adaptive time-step and refined grids in selected regions to efficiently handle large interface movements. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we conducted several tests, including a water tank experiment, demonstrating its ability to accurately predict both simple and tank-filling scenarios.

In multiagent learning settings, learning outcomes are typically evaluated based on the ability to reach an equilibrium in a transformed game, where transformed games involve re-distributing the payoffs among the agents. This is relevant because it can lead to more equitable reward distribution among the agents and prevent a single agent from receiving all the reward for discovering valuable joint strategies. This work delves into equilibrium concepts, such as Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE), where individual payoffs can't always be concealed, and it's not always feasible to divide the payoff according to a Nash Social Welfare Maximization (NSWM) principle. The primary contribution of this work is to frame the challenge of learning CCE and CE as policy recommendation problems, and to show that existing method's reward allocation techniques, which distribute rewards based on the social welfare, are suboptimal. Furthermore, it's shown that these methods can't effectively learn CCE or CE, and existing approaches, such as MultiAgent Counterfactual Value Learning (MACVL), are proven to be reward-inefficient, and it's also demonstrated that the reward allocation in CE can't always be arranged to maximize the social welfare.

An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible-Infected model is conducted on an infinite binary tree, with infections spreading randomly to neighboring nodes based on a coin flip, and recoveries occurring when infected nodes become susceptible. As the coin flip's bias changes, the model exhibits highly variable behavior, and in the infected phase, the fraction of permanently infected nodes shows dramatic fluctuations over time. At a critical coin flip value, these variations become significant enough to suggest an infinite distribution, and similar results can be observed in a related model without restarts. A new approach, combining the influence of past events and stochastic processes, is used to analyze these results, building on previous research and related works in the field of stochastic processes and statistical physics.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple interacting components, reinforcement learning agents can collaborate and share data.  However, traditional reinforcement learning is hindered by limited sample efficiency.  Due to its high computational cost, exploiting new states consumes a lot of computational resources, making it necessary to relearn from previously visited states.  Classical experience replay shares the past data to accelerate learning, but it's ineffective with large-scale systems as it requires multiple optimization steps to navigate them.  A novel reinforcement learning framework called Fiedler Replay Accelerated Policy Learning (FRAPAL) is proposed, which utilizes the past data without consumption, combining spectral graph theory and reinforcement learning.  FRAPAL leverages the historical experience stored in a weighted adjacency matrix, focusing on states closely connected in the data graph.  Theoretical analysis and numerical results demonstrate the accuracy and fast convergence of FRAPAL, outperforming classical experience replay and classical policy learning methods in both synthetic and real-world tests.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face varying levels of cooperation from dialogue partners, who may have different intentions. To facilitate research, we've created the MultiTalk Dataset, comprising over 14,000 dialogue transcripts that depict conversations where participants have different goals. Our analysis reveals that effective dialogue management requires understanding the partner's goal and that simple machine learning models can successfully accomplish task-oriented dialogue under these complex conditions.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool designed to facilitate complex simulations of cosmology under modified gravitational theories. MG-GLAM extends the capabilities of our previous public code, MG-RAM, by adding support for an array of modified gravity models including f(R), Yukawa, Chameleon, and Power-Law frameworks. These models are incorporated into N-body simulations using a second-order perturbation approach and the Newtonian approximation, allowing us to capture the non-linear evolution of matter distribution under modified gravity. MG-GLAM is built upon the highly efficient spectral code, MG-RAM, and includes features such as live particle masses, variable time steps, and binary tree algorithms to optimize performance. We provide detailed examples of modified gravity model implementations and offer the code's source as well as installation instructions to the research community.

Established in 1998 by Carmona, Scherpa, and Aldous, a profound connection was discovered between the Dyson model of interparticlar distances and the Gaussian free field (GFF). Building upon a similar work by Biskup, I will extend this relationship to a novel setting that combines elements of the Dyson model at equilibrium and out of equilibrium, specifically for the case of beta=2. This novel setting forms a bridge between these two previously identified scenarios and also incorporates a profound connection with logarithmically correlated fields.

MediaWiki, an open-source wiki platform, enables multiple users to create and edit a shared set of web-based documents.
The popular wiki editor 'WorkingWiki' extends MediaWiki with a sophisticated interface and collaborative features, making it suitable for in-depth collaboration on complex projects, including software development.
The codebase of WorkingWiki itself serves as an exemplary project demonstrating its capabilities.
The codebase primarily consists of JavaScript, with supplementary components in PHP, and is well-documented, allowing new contributors to easily navigate and understand the project.
The developers have established clear guidelines for code contributions, including the use of specific tools like ESLint and Prettier for maintaining coding standards.
The repository's history and evolution are transparently recorded, with key milestones and contributors documented in the project's history file.
Overall, the codebase of WorkingWiki is highly collaborative, well-maintained, and serves as a valuable resource for developers working on similar projects.

This study investigates the impact of flame temperature fluctuations on the generation of turbulence heat release fluctuations, a factor often overlooked in current linear stochastic flow models and theories of thermoacoustic instability. We establish a nonlinear stochastic flame model that considers the burning velocity fluctuation response to acoustic pressure and includes the effect of thermal noise and flame tapering. Through direct numerical simulation (DNS) of a planar jet flow at Re_lambda = 10000, the model's output is compared and found to match the actual temperature fluctuations. Furthermore, our results show that ignoring the influence of flame temperature on temperature fluctuations can lead to inaccurate assessments of sound generation, especially in the higher frequency range.

We investigate the impact of an ultra-light dark matter field on the neutrinoless double beta decay mediated by the $N_{R1}$ right-handed neutrino in a minimal next-to-seesaw model. In a specific cosmological setting, where the dark matter is composed of an ultralight scalar field oscillating around a minimum, a term in the neutrino mass matrix periodically interacts with the neutrinoless double beta decay process through a mixing term with a right-handed neutrino. This results in both explicit and nonexplicit neutrino flavor, leading to distinctive signatures that could potentially be detected in a single experiment's data. In contrast to standard neutrinoless double beta decay signals, these signatures do not enhance or suppress decay rates but rather shift their positions. In certain parameter ranges, this shift in position can be as large as 1 TeV, and in combination with other constraints, it may help determine the identity of the N$_{R1}$ right-handed neutrino. In addition to this, we also examine the impact of an ultralight axion like dark matter on the neutrinoless double beta decay mediated by the $N_{R1}$ right-handed neutrino. In both scenarios, we provide estimates for the allowed parameter space where these interactions do not significantly impact the observed neutrinoless double beta decay half-life.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory.
It modifies gravity by adding a nonlocal term to the Ricci tensor, which can be seen as an extra dimension of space in a finite distance from the original space.
This term is a key component of the field equations and can be replaced with a higher order tensor in another space that has the same basic characteristics as the original space.
We show that nonlocal gravity theory is equivalent to asymptotically AdS extra dimension theory in a recent change of basis.
This connection is made through the Geyer-Ahmed master action, which includes both four dimensional gravity and the two additional dimensions of a finite distance in a lower distance space.
By applying a specific type of field theory reduction to the Geyer-Ahmed action, we derive the nonlocal gravity action.
This connection is made through the Geyer-Ahmed master action, which includes both four dimensional gravity and the two additional dimensions of a finite distance in a lower distance space.

Understanding how and why certain genetic variations influence human characteristics remains a complex challenge. By combining population data from 502 individuals with functional data from DNase-I hypersensitive sites, researchers have developed a new method to pinpoint regulatory regions in the genome. This new categorization technique, along with an examination of existing evidence, reveals that genetic variations influencing height, blood traits, and other characteristics are heavily concentrated within these regulatory regions. Moreover, these associations vary depending on the specific trait being studied, with immune-related and brain-related features displaying the strongest connections in these regions, while variations affecting blood traits show little to no connection. Ultimately, this study provides a vital foundation for further research into the functional aspects of the genome associated with specific human characteristics.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC involving small systems studied
by the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Due to the growing significance
of QCD in small systems, particularly in events with high transverse momentum,
investigations into possible connections between small and large systems are
particularly relevant. This relevance is highlighted by the observation of
collective phenomena in small systems. This work will review findings related
to particle production in proton-proton, proton-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus
collisions at high energies, with a focus on results from the ATLAS and ALICE
collaborations. A summary of key observations made by the ATLAS collaboration
in relation to particle production patterns will be presented, along with the
related work undertaken by the ALICE collaboration. This work will also
examine the origin of flow in hadronic and hadron-nucleus collisions, as well
as hadron-nucleus collisions in various geometries. A discussion on hadron
resonance decay and hadronization models will be included. A review of other
production patterns and hadronization models will be provided, along with an
analysis of hadronic flow in heavy ion collisions. A summary of open questions
and possible future research directions will be presented.

Observations of some well-known, frequently recurring low mass X-ray binaries with Einstein rings suggest that their transient bursts may be associated with the complete consumption of a neutron star by its parent object. Astronomers have previously hypothesized that transient LMXBs with very long intervals - years to decades - might be caused by the recent absorption of a neutron star by a sub-stellar mass companion, such as a planet or a brown dwarf. However, existing data only supports recurrence times up to 10 years, falling short of what's needed to validate this theory. Utilizing recurrence times from 100 years to 10 million years found in literature, we have estimated the minimum mass of the companion object for each burst and discovered that their distribution peaks between 0.05 and 0.1 M_sun, which corresponds to the mass range of neutron star devouring candidates. This may indicate that the majority of LMXBs with a wide recurrence time range may in fact be low mass objects that have already been classified.

THz radiation allows for the exploration of a system's ground state and low-lying excitations, making it an invaluable tool for nonlinear spectroscopy. As the nonlinear response of deeply bound electrons requires a driving field of THz frequency, combining this with optical fields enables researchers to investigate coupled nonler responses in the infrared spectrum. While various methods exist for trapping ions and electrons, circular motion induces inertial effects that induce significant red shifts in vibrational and rotational frequencies, altering the vibrational and rotational properties of molecules and shifting energy levels in atoms. Although the influence of circular motion on energy levels has been examined in several studies, its impact on the nonlinear susceptibility is still unclear. To address this knowledge gap, we calculated the inertial contributions to the third-order susceptibility tensor, accounting for both circular motion's effect on dipole operators and energy level shifts. Considering the magnitude of THz and optical fields, we focused on a scalar component of the susceptibility tensor, but its calculation can be extended to all tensor components. Using a coherent superposition of three models - the two-center, three-center, and four-center models - of an atom or molecule with two, three, and four ionized centers and trapped electrons, we examined the susceptibility tensor. Our results show that the third-order susceptibility tensor is highly sensitive to circular behavior, with a significant increase in magnitude observed in both solid and gaseous states. This enhanced third-order susceptibility tensor may enable the study of coherent wave mixing in gas using only THz

Improving the diversity of neural conversational agents' responses remains a challenging task. To address this issue, we introduce a novel assessment framework based on Natural Language inference, which provides a more comprehensive evaluation of response diversity than current evaluation methods. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough examination of existing models' performance using our framework, revealing the variability in reported Natural Language inference-based diversity metrics found in previous studies. As the existing diversity evaluation methods are found to be inadequate, we propose two new, simple yet effective evaluation methods that guarantee the statistical properties of diversity measures are met. Our proposed assessment framework and evaluation methods, when applied to existing diverse conversational datasets, provide a more precise benchmark for future research.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning can be significantly impacted in very low-mass stellar objects with rotation, potentially hindering it, particularly as the object's angular velocity increases beyond a critical threshold where surface angular velocities of slow rotating stars are found. Despite this finding, it is unlikely that prominent effects observed in protostars indicate they are rotating faster than this critical rate. As the angular velocity exceeds this limit, the minimum mass necessary for sustained hydrogen burning increases, particularly as hydrogen is confined to a thinner spherical shell within the object rather than a thicker layer or a central core. Moreover, hydrogen burning in this shell releases less energy than in the core of a typical low-mass star, necessitating more intense convection in its underlying layers.

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, 
but it's constrained by specific instrumental influences that can distort the results. 
These constraints include the efficiency of particle detection, momentum measurements 
of decay products, and various other factors that can impact the analysis. 
To overcome these challenges, statisticians have developed sophisticated methods, 
but each comes with its own set of strengths and weaknesses. 
This review covers three primary techniques: matrix element methods, 
per-event weighting, and multivariate methods, which are commonly used in amplitude 
analyses. 
It discusses the strengths and weaknesses of each method and provides relevant 
examples from LHC experiments to illustrate their applications.

A new model for radiation energy dynamics in coexpanding matter and radiation is introduced, featuring distinct phases - a vigorous fireball and a phase with moderate intensity. The model's equations of motion are derived and applied to study gamma-ray emissions from three types of astronomical objects, including short and long gamma-ray bursts, blazars, and $\gamma$-ray pulsars. For each object, the model predicts the energy, spectral characteristics, and peak luminosity of emitted $\gamma$-rays. Notably, the emissions from a $\gamma$-ray burst (GRB 030327D) and blazar (BLR 1111+084) exceed Eddington limits, and the model posits that some very high energy $\gamma$-ray emissions from blazars may trigger the formation of relativistic jets.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct categories of objects have numerous applications in fields like biology and chemistry.  When representing these graphs, the number of crossings between lines should be as low as possible to enhance clarity and understanding.  In this paper, an efficient technique is introduced to compute the minimum number of crossings for specific types of bipartite graphs, with a focus on sparse connections.  The proposed method counts intersections in an initial layout and performs local modifications to achieve the smallest possible crossings, without increasing their number, using a straightforward data structure to achieve optimal computational efficiency.

This paper presents a novel approach to bipedal walking that incorporates dynamic thrust generated by a robot's thrusters. By combining an inverse dynamics model with optimization techniques, we developed a method to compute gait trajectories that minimize the effort required and account for balance, thrust, and joint limits. The results of our research were tested through numerical simulations, specifically using the NASA JPL's 3DPrint robot, and demonstrated the ability to execute stable walks with varying thrust levels and external disturbances. The inclusion of thrust as a balance-achieving actuator provides a significant advancement over previous methods that relied on linear models.

Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first established the surjectivity of the total residue map for finite fields $k$ in their paper "Linear forms and the Milnor K-theory of valued fields". This research extended these results by demonstrating that the degree of the residue map in its associated morphism from a variety over a perfect field $k$ is linked to the rank of the variety, in relation to the equation y^n = f(x_1,...,x_d). This extension was motivated in part by a linear form theorem proposed by Poonen and Reichstein. Building on these foundations, we further developed this theory by proving that the surjectivity found by Becker, Denef, and Lipschitz holds true for valued fields over any field $k$, in their article "Linear forms and the Milnor K-theory of valued fields".

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, named SMTPerf, that leverages performance characteristics of simultaneous multithreading architectures.  Unlike previous methods, which manipulated architectural or microarchitectural features, SMTPerf exploits the behavior of SMT to manipulate resource contention and schedule delays across multiple threads.  By manipulating this behavior, multiple systems operating on multiple cores can be forced to exhibit varied timing patterns, thereby causing an attacker to incorrectly deduce the target victim's true data.  To make this innovative technique possible, the researchers customized the Parallels Workstation 2 virtualization software to manipulate scheduling and threading settings of multiple systems.  Experimental results, conducted using 10 different configurations across multiple systems, showed that a minimal investment of side-channel resources could be made to steal valuable information from a target victim.  Specifically, one system operating on a single core, could accurately classify data of another system, operating on a single core, with a 100 times larger dataset, following a side-channel attack with a classification accuracy of 99.99 percent.  Furthermore, the researchers found that the performance degradation caused by the technique was substantial, resulting in an 8 times decrease in application execution time.  Due to the widespread adoption of SMT architectures in modern computers and servers, the researchers believe that their technique could be highly effective in a variety of real-world scenarios.

A topological rule that transforms a knot into the trivial unknot through a finite sequence of specific moves is known as an unknotting sequence. This paper introduces a method to modify the Jones polynomial using just two moves called inverse conjugation and addition, thereby yielding polynomials for knots that can be transformed into the basic unknot through these specific steps. It is demonstrated that applying the Jones polynomial's unknotting algorithm requires at most $4n-2$ moves, where $n$ denotes the highest power of variable involved. Furthermore, it is shown that any knot whose Jones polynomial matches that of the $(3,10)$-torus knot requires at least 11 of the allowed moves to resolve into the basic unknot, thereby proving that this polynomial adheres to a rigorous criterion called the stable genus property. Additionally, it is discovered that the Jones polynomial's required moves to resolve a knot matches exactly that of the torus genus of that same knot.

We've demonstrated that combining the Gassner invariant and the order it is assessed by, creates a Vassiliev invariant of the first kind for colored braids, specifically of the first vessel for braids and of the second type for brabs. This combines a view from the first kind of Vassiliev invariants and the second kind of Vassiliev invariants. Furthermore, we've deduced the specific formulas for the initial coefficients of this invariant, including the Gassner invariant of the boundary braids in a colored braid, as well as the order it is assessed by, equivalent to the sum of the braid's winding numbers.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination is a key factor that determines success in executing tasks. We propose a new framework called NE-Coach, which integrates reinforcement learning and game theory to teach agents to effectively coordinate on complex tasks. Our approach involves two stages: initially, we employ a state-of-the-art method for joint-action attention to teach the agents to collaborate based on shared task information, and subsequently, we employ a policy that considers individual rewards to encourage a stable and efficient solution. Our experiments across various scenarios with different task complexities and environments, using both simple and complex settings, show that our two-stage policy produces a stable environment with a balanced combination of individual and collective considerations, resulting in an improved understanding of complex settings and an overall setting that is more in tune with the settings we started with.

This work is an in-depth study on federated learning variations, specifically focusing on horizontal and vertical FL. We develop mathematical models for both FL types, examine their commonalities and differences, and analyze their special cases. A comprehensive taxonomy is presented to categorize all FL scenarios. Additionally, references to existing research on FL, privacy-enhancing techniques, and differential data volumes in FL are provided. This article serves as a valuable resource and starting point for both FL and multi-party collaboration problems.

Kernel methods are widely used in machine learning due to their strong
performance on various tasks, including classification, support vector
classification, and SVM.  However, their application to large scale datasets
is severely limited by the $O(n^2)$ memory requirement and training time,
which both scale quadratically with the number of data points.  To overcome
this limitation, researchers have developed various kernel approximations,
such as random features, that reduce both memory usage and training time to
linear scale.  Despite these advancements, the field lacks a unified,
comprehensive framework that encompasses all existing linear kernel methods,
making it challenging to compare their effectiveness and scalability.  To fill
this gap, we present Linear Kernel Methods Unified (LKMU), a comprehensive
framework that integrates all existing linear kernel methods, providing a
standardized approach to evaluating their performance and scalability across
different datasets and problem types.  By implementing LKMU and applying it
to a wide range of datasets and problems, we identify the strengths and
weaknesses of various linear kernel methods, enabling researchers to easily
compare their effectiveness and scalability.  LKMU is available as an
open-source project on GitHub at https://github.com/ChengShi01/LKMU.

In our study, we've identified a group isomorphism between a specific group composed of wreath products in group theory and a groups-wreath-products-in-groups isomorphism. This isomorphism holds true when applying to both sides in a variety setting, resulting in a declaration for groups and monoids in monads.

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n≥4) within a hypersphere of a higher dimension of n+2 space. We start by classifying and describing these hypersurfaces with constant M"obius curvature under a specific condition involving the gradient of a function. Next, we identify the compact conformally flat hypersurfaces with constant M"obius curvature. Finally, we determine the Riemannian geometry of these hypersurfaces with constant M"obius curvature. A specific type of map, the Nirenberg map, is central to these analyses.
