Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions matching our findings. Both steady and time-varying drives resulted in both theoretical and computed results aligning closely, validating the effectiveness of the path integral method used.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by altering their rotational periods and spinning rates through the modification of thermal radiation patterns caused by rotational and orbital factors. As a result, these effects can potentially lead to the breakup of an asteroid. In this study, we utilized a numerical model to simulate the YORP effect based on the finite-element method, which allowed us to take into account complex patterns of thermal radiation. By inputting data from three asteroids - Mathilde, Steins, and Ryugu - we were able to estimate YORP coefficients and compare them to previous research findings. Our results showed YORP coefficients of -0.64e-9 m/s/rot for Mathilde, 2.02e-9 m/s/rot for Steins, and 9.5e-10 m/s/rot for Ryugu, which are within the estimated ranges reported in the literature.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

In this paper, we examine whether or not regular functions defined on metric spaces are both computably and continuously mapped. We prove that such functions are indeed continuously mapped, and if the input space has a computably represented metric and the output is a finite set, we show that the function is computably mapped. However, if the input space is an infinite Baire class one compact set with a computable metric, we're able to create a counterexample demonstrating that there exists a pathing function that isn't continuously mapped.

A machine learning technique called reservoir computing generates a precise, artificial sense of place by finding a complex relationship between current and past inputs. Next-generation reservoir computing aims to simplify this model for more efficient processing on related hardware. We propose a more efficient variant of this technique that uses more robust signal processing and can achieve more accurate predictions with less data. Compared to existing methods, our variant can become trained with a complex model that finds a complex pattern without getting stuck in a complex, circular pattern. It also has the ability to accurately forecast signals that vary in time and space, including variations in both the frequency and location of these patterns.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This algorithm, which determines the set of states that can reach a target within a certain time frame while considering disturbances and staying in an allowable region, was made to work efficiently by combining its solutions through variational principles. Our custom data structure, which combines a grid with a sparse representation of the state space, enables fast computation even in high-dimensional state spaces. Test cases have shown that this approach can accurately produce the reachable state space for a ten-dimensional state space, which can handle millions of states in a reasonable amount of time.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain a subject of debate, with various studies showing both gradual and abrupt changes along the animacy spectrum. We propose that the observed animacy patterns in neural responses may result from either distinct populations of stimuli being processed or from the complexity of processing being gradually increasing. To test these possibilities, we used natural images and video stimuli with differing levels of animacy, ranging from inanimate objects to humans. Our results, supported by both population and single-neuron analyses, indicate that an abrupt, cortical organization best explains the observed animacy patterns in the ventral temporal cortex. Notably, our findings suggest that the majority of V4 and IT neurons respond more strongly to animate than inanimate stimuli, further supporting the animate superiority hypothesis.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, supported by the broader conclusion that Dirichlet L-function zeros exert a force pushing zeros from all other automorphic L-functions off the s=1 axis.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs.

The rapid global spread of COVID-19 has highlighted the complex relationship between the virus's inherent contagiousness and various social factors, such as human behavior and transmission patterns. While epidemiological models have been used to study these dynamics, they often overlook the impact of "super-spreader events," where a single infected individual infects a disproportionately high number of people. To address this gap, we developed an $SIR$ model that incorporates these events, allowing for an estimation of the effective base reproduction number, $R_0$, based on data from confirmed cases. By analyzing the relationship between the time-varying reproduction number, $R_t$, and $R_0$, we found that the distribution of transmission clusters can be described using Cox's proportional hazards model. This allowed us to estimate $R_0$ and investigate its relationship with $R_t$. Our findings suggest that most transmission events result in $R_t$ values below 1, and that $R_0$ is heavily influenced by super-spreader events. We observed that $R_0$ was effectively lowered in regions with stricter containment measures, such as Hubei, and that variations in $R_t$ were more pronounced in the early stages of the epidemic. Ultimately, our study provides valuable insights into the epidemiological dynamics of COVID-19 and the importance of understanding the impact of super-spreader events.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper seeks to expand the concept of codiskcyclicity, initially defined for a single operator within L(X), to a set of operators W \subseteq L(X). It provides characterizations of what it means for sets of operators to be codiskcyclic or even strongly codiskcyclic, particularly when they act on an invariant subspace of X. Furthermore, it codiskcyclicity and strong codiskcyclicity for sets of operators are explored, with relevant examples and applications provided. This research builds upon and enhances the concept of a single operator having a codiskcyclic characteristic.

The study examined the BiAs in the measurement of the magnetic field's component perpendicular to the line-of-sight (Delta B_perp) using Strong Magnetic Fields (SMFs) in the Sun's photosphere, as observed through the inversion of Spectral Lines (SLs). We analyzed three SLs (Ca II 8542 A, Fe I 15648 A, and Fe I 15652 A) commonly used in the Least Squares Inversion (LSI) method, in four SMAs (BiAs samples) with known Llongitudes, where we calculated the oscillating BiAs (Delta B_perp) caused by the Earth's rotation. We found that the LLSI method produces a significant biAs in the derived values of Delta B_perp, with values up to 25 G, which is attributed to the interaction between the static longitudinal magnetic field and the terrestrial oscillating field, creating an erroneous triAs component. Our findings show that this biAs becomes more pronounced with higher frequencies of the LLSI method, and is heavily influenced by the field strength and observation latitude. To mitigate this biAs, we suggest using SLs with low effective charges, and we also discuss the impact of other effects, such as Doppler broadening and circular polarization, on the LLSI biAs.

A sign problem has been successfully mitigated in a specific region of the parameter space through reweighting and constraint exclusion techniques in a Monte Carlo study of (1+1)D N_r N_t lattice Euclidean time.  However, the reweighting and constraint exclusion methods both result in an exponential increase in the sign problem as filling levels differ from half-filling.  Our study found that both techniques remain computationally feasible well beyond these filling levels, even as temperature and coupling become smaller.  A moderate decrease in time step leads to signal-to-noise ratios that grow exponentially with system size, which can be counteracted through reweighting.  Ultimately, a numerical overhead is left that is not dependent on time step or density.  Our results are applicable to various applications, including Hubbard models used to describe superconductivity and charge transfer processes.

Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image subshift Y under σ and the associated complexity functions p_X and p_Y exhibit the following relationship: there exist constants C and D such that p_Y exhibits growth relative to p_X, specifically p_X displays slower or equal growth compared to p_Y for sufficiently large values of n.

By leveraging previously acquired skills, we can enable language models to handle new or unfamiliar tasks without the need for additional training, a concept known as cross-task generalization. However, due to the vast number of possible tasks and their diverse requirements, identifying relevant skills and effectively combining them for solving a new problem is a significant challenge. To address this issue, we investigate the potential of using simple loss functions that focus on a single skill at a time, a method we call MultiTaskSingleTaskLearning. Our approach, which uses the MARIO dataset, demonstrates that our learning strategy, called MultiTaskSingleTaskLearning, results in models with enhanced performance, allowing them to excel in various evaluations, including the CMARIO benchmark, where our model outperforms the baseline T5 in several categories, and an external benchmark, LAGIA, called to assess the models' ability to solve complex multi-step algebraic problems, a task our model is able to solve with a significant level of accuracy, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue that has not yet been thoroughly addressed. In this paper, we investigate parameter tuning for a private model and evaluate the feasibility of employing popular hyperparameter optimization algorithms while adhering to data privacy standards. We specifically assess the performance of a private version of grid search, random hyperparameter selection, and random hyperparameter optimization algorithms under the DPSGD framework. To provide a comprehensive understanding, we present a detailed analysis of the DPSGD setting and the impacts of data perturbation on hyperparameter optimization algorithms, as well as practical tips for implementing a successful private hyperparameter optimization process.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of all distinct elements within an isotypic Worb under the equivalence relation that maps Ssb W to subsets of S. When applied to Wreath Product types, this approach allows us to determine that the homotopy type of this boolean complex is equivalent to a set of spheres, specifically 24d−2 spheres, under certain conditions. Furthermore, we identify a substantial subset of W that forms a basis for the homology of this boolean complex, and similarly, for subsets of S under which this subset is invariant, we find that the corresponding homology group is isomorphic to a vector space with a specific basis.

We applied an advanced statistical method, known as Discrete Principal Component Analysis (DPCA), to investigate elemental compositions in 164 globular clusters from the Milky Way using data from the APOGEE-2 survey. Our goal was to better understand the chemical history of our galaxy's stellar population by analyzing chemical patterns associated with different types of stars and understanding the origins of various elements. As a result, we found that different types of stellar explosions, specifically Type II and Type Ia supernovae, are responsible for different elemental compositions in globular clusters. Specifically, we determined that supernovii type II events, such as supernovii, neutron star mergers, and gamma-ray bursts, are primarily responsible for the "prompt" elemental compositions in clusters, including oxygen, magnesium, silicon, and iron. On the other hand, supernovii type Ia events, which occur in binary star systems, are primarily responsible for the "delayed" compositions in clusters, including elements like titanium, chromium, and manganese. By using various indicators, we were able to distinguish between the "prompt" and "delayed" components in these clusters, and found that they are closely related to specific features in the periodic table, such as iron-peak elements and alpha elements. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020, accompanied by a surge in misinformation, particularly on social media platforms. Online rumors pose a significant threat to public health crises, distorting information dissemination and exacerbating the crisis. This study investigates the mechanisms of online rumor propagation, combining theoretical analysis, simulation, and empirical data. We examine the relationship between online and offline information dissemination, focusing on the COVID-19 pandemic. Our research reveals that COVID-19-related rumors propagate at different rates across different media channels, with significant variations observed across different countries. Our growth rate matrix captures the dynamic propagation behavior of online rumors and provides a foundation for developing more accurate propagation models. This study contributes to the understanding of online rumor propagation, providing new insights and data-driven findings to advance the field.

A novel technique for estimating galaxy distances has been proposed by researchers, relying on the planetary nebula phase within the post-AGB evolution of stars. This method utilizes the strong [O III] emission lines to determine absolute line fluxes and, by applying the Phillips relation, it's possible to calculate line ratios and ultimately estimate the distance to the host galaxy. Analyzing nine previously known galaxies through this lens, along with four newly discovered hosts, reveals an average discrepancy of approximately 10 percent when compared to established distance measurements. This finding supports the validity of using P-N methods for estimating distances to galaxies.

Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from patients, which is critical for making swift and informed medical decisions. Despite this, manually analyzing such data is both time-consuming and prone to errors. To address these challenges, we present LifeStream, a real-time processing system that can handle structured data in a stream format. LifeStream specializes in processing physiological data, offering an optimized engine that significantly accelerates query execution while providing a simple interface for writing streaming code. By tapping into multiple data sources, LifeStream can join real-time data with historical records and perform complex temporal analyses to detect critical events, such as sudden drops in blood pressure, immediately upon occurrence. Testing these features on large datasets demonstrates LifeStream's superior performance compared to traditional streaming engines, especially in processing joined queries and temporal aggregations, while also showing a high degree of efficiency in terms of energy consumption.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function in training a DNN for classified is an important decision that significantly affects the model's performance. This study evaluates the effectiveness of various loss functions, both traditional and innovative, across multiple datasets and classification tasks. By systematically testing multiple loss functions simultaneously, the study aims to identify the most suitable function for each task. The results show significant differences in model performance when using different loss functions, with traditional methods like softmax and pairwise being outperformed by novel approaches such as pairwise squared. A heat map is developed to visualize the relationship between loss functions and classification tasks, helping researchers and practitioners select the most appropriate loss function for their specific needs.

This research paper examines the thermal and mechanical characteristics of polyethylene subjected to induced crystallization through various methods. Strain-induced crystallization, in particular, significantly alters a polymer's mechanical and thermal properties, making it essential to understand the underlying mechanisms. We combine inelastic theory with molecular dynamics simulations to investigate strain-induced phase transitions and crystallization, focusing on the mechanical behavior of the resulting material. Our analysis reveals that, at the molecular level, crystalline regions form and become interconnected as the material is stretched, ultimately leading to phase transformation. We also observe that the crystalline structure influences the polymer's mechanical properties, which in turn affect the material's response to further stretching. Notably, we find that the polymer's side groups affect the material's response to strain, which is demonstrated by comparing low and high molecular weight polyethylene. Finally, we provide guidance on how to design simulations that accurately reflect mechanical tests performed on real materials.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly robust against various impairments, such as frequency and phase errors caused by imperfect synchronization, as well as Doppler shifts and time-varying scattering patterns. Nevertheless, this method requires a significantly larger bandwidth compared to coherent detection methods and demands minimal bit error rate performance. This work delves into the structure of optimal decision rules for differential detection, which can be represented as linear combinations of consecutive differentiable differential symbols, guided by an underlying dynamic programming framework. Furthermore, it demonstrates through numerical analysis that for BPSK-CPM with two-symbol differential periods, the ideal non-linear decision rule can be accurately emulated using a two-symbol system, whereas for M-ary CPM variants, the required differentiable symbol duration grows logarithmically with M. Notably, this analysis provides an explanation for the prevalent choice of a three-symbol duration in current differential CPM modem implementations.

A recent study examined the variance of energy density around its mean value, a fundamental thermodynamic measure of fluctuations, which is closely linked to specific heat and specific to quantum systems. A discrete model was developed to illustrate how the variance can be expressed in terms of the Vassiliev invariants of braids, a specific type of mathematical object, by utilizing the Vassiliev's approach to construct a cohomology theory for braids. This approach was further refined using the Vassiliev's vacuum value method. The research also delved into the Varchenko's approach to define a determinant value for a specific matrix associated with braids, a method that generalizes Vassiliev's approach and vacuum value method. This generalization was found to satisfy the same cohomology relations as the Vassiliev's approach, thereby providing the Vassiliev's approach with a concrete basis in the context of Varchenko's determinant value method. The study's findings were validated through the Vassiliev's vacuum value method and the Varchenko's determinant value method, both of which supported the Vassiliev's approach's vacuum value method and cohomology relations. The research was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under grant number 11971337.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an extensive collection of 1.3 million pairs of everyday actions and following actions that naturally occur after the first actions. We incorporate this action-reasoning knowledge into our category of implicit relations in the Natural Language Inference (NLI) task and investigate the impact of action-reasoning implications on the intention identification task. We outline the challenges of identifying implicit intentions from action-reasoning follow-ups and provide guidance for creating a robust intention dataset free from action-implication biases.

Portfolio optimization is a critical task in finance, heavily relying on accurate and timely risk estimates. This study leverages portfolio variance's quadratic characteristic to explore how the HHL quantum algorithm can efficiently determine optimal asset allocation. By examining both constant and time-varying risk scenarios, we identify the method's computational complexities across different market conditions. Furthermore, our analysis considers various portfolio choices under constant risk, revealing the portfolio variance minimization requires significant quantum computational resources. In contrast, under time-varying risk, our study reveals the portfolio variance minimization requires moderate to significant quantum computational resources, depending on the market scenario. Ultimately, our research provides precise quantum computational conditions for finding the most efficient portfolio allocation.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models, we plan to investigate a comprehensive framework for using a complete set of ASR auxiliary tasks in a multi-modal approach. However, this comes with two significant challenges. Firstly, selecting the most suitable auxiliary tasks from numerous options that can boost performance, and secondly, effectively fusing the speech representations learned from these tasks. To address these challenges, we propose an attention-based fusion method and a carefully chosen multi-task configuration. Evaluations on three public datasets, LiAR, AMI, and CallHome, with limited annotated speech data, show that our proposed method significantly improves performance, particularly on smaller datasets, and is more robust than other baselines.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1), \dots, \pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and uniformly distributed in the set $\{1, \dots, n\}$, where $k_n$ can grow as fast as $\log n$. As a contrast, we also analyze the asymptotic distribution of parking functions conditioned to be uniformly random rather than uniformly random subject to conditions.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires with a strong disorder have revealed the presence of a localized insulating state. As the nanowires undergo a transition from their superconducting state to their localized insulating state, the critical current density required triggers the formation of a moving step. This movement leads to a blockade of direct current conduction, characteristic of a phase slip. The analysis of data from these experiments has shown that the blockades follow an exponential distribution, with an average block length that decreases as the critical current density increases. The data also indicates that the blockades become more massive as the critical current density rises, providing strong evidence in support of the Grossman-Raelson-Rothstein theory, which suggests that the blockades eventually become massive enough to destroy superconductivity at higher current densities.

Our proposed approach, known as NeRV2VP, tackles the challenge of creating view-change videos for mobile devices by transforming them from slow to rapid movements. Our method takes an input video from any angle and generates multiple future viewpoints, even from significantly different angles up to 90 degrees. In contrast to existing techniques, NeRV2VP, which is a extension of NeRF, differs from existing end-to-end video-to-video prediction techniques. Our solution, which is an improvement on previous end-to-end video-to-video prediction approaches, is also distinct. Our proposed approach, known as NeRV2VP, tackles the challenge of creating view-change videos from perspectives ranging from slight to significant differences. Our method, which is an extension of NeRF, differs from existing end-to-end prediction techniques by encoding the entire input video, rather than just a single frame, in a proposed video neural field. Our solution, which is an enhancement on previous end-to-end prediction approaches, is also unique. Our NeRV2VP model, which is a time-aware representation, is able to represent the 3D scene, including its dynamic components, by learning the relationship between different viewing angles and time. Our NeRV2VP model, which is a comprehensive framework, is also capable of using static views to predict unseen angles and dynamic views to forecast future perspectives, which is a significant step forward from existing methods.
