High-precision ground-based telescopes are now conducting a new type of astrometric analysis, which accounts for general relativistic effects. Building on a previous study by us, we investigated how a departure from unity in the post-Newtonian parameter gamma influences estimated parallaxes in Section II, and demonstrated that this deviation results in a linearly proportional shift in parallax values, which can be seen as a distinct signal gamma provides. In II A, we specifically explored CGGS theory, and in II B, we utilized the post-Birkhoff radiations model to illustrate our approach. In Section III, we offered a solution to the Einstein field equations within this model's framework. We then applied our solution to the Birkhoff theorem in the context of gamma and discovered that the unique gravitational potential generated by any mass distribution becomes both non-zero and dependent on that mass when gamma differs from unity. Finally, in Sections IV and V, we examined four distinct cases: four-dimensional spacetime without gravity, two additional post-Birkhoff models, and three additional radiations models.

Utilizing external knowledge to enhance answers to questions based on common sense is a difficult task. This is particularly true when dealing with vast knowledge bases, as it becomes increasingly difficult to manually verify the relevance and correctness of associated factual statements. Furthermore, multiple irrelevant or incorrect facts can confuse retrieval-based models and lead to inaccurate answers. In order to overcome these challenges, we present CoQAIE, a model based on attention mechanisms that can effectively filter out irrelevant and incorrect knowledge from the available background statements in the Social Commonsense Question Answering dataset. CoQAIE utilizes a two-stage knowledge retrieval process, which has shown significant performance improvements over the baseline model and state-of-the-art methods in the CoQA dataset, as evidenced by our results of 40.06 CERC and 36.72 SQuAD scores.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are warm and rich in photons, which may facilitate the formation of molecular cations like N2+, NO+, and CO+. These cations have short lifespans in these environments, limiting their accumulation to low concentrations that might be detectable through observations of comets. Although previous studies have explored the possible presence of these species, a comprehensive understanding of their comprehensive combustion dynamics has been hindered by a lack of combustion data for specific electronic states. In this research, we have filled this gap by producing a variety of molecular cations, including N2+, NO+, and CO+, via pulsed laser techniques and combining their neutral counterparts with helium gas in a dual laser post mass spectrometer, and we have measured their combustion dynamics through delayed extraction mass spectrometry. The results reveal that the N2+ first and second electronic states have relatively long lifespans, with a combustion duration of approximately 10 milliseconds, while for NO+, the longer-lived state has a combustion duration of approximately 30 milliseconds, and CO+, which only has a short electronic state, has a combustion duration of approximately 1 microsecond.

A significant challenge in deploying a distributed system for learning is the uneven spread of data across different nodes. A critical issue in Federated Learning relates to this non-IID data distribution, as the personal models are influenced by the varying quality of the data. A novel approach is proposed in this work, utilizing a reinforcement learning algorithm to identify and prioritize updates from models trained on high-quality, IID data. The proposed method is validated through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in comparing to a traditional model aggregation technique.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health issues, yet little research has examined how non-pharmacological mental health treatments, such as therapy, impact the behavior of offenders. To fill this research gap, we analyze the effect of face-to-face court-mandated mental health treatments on a cohort of Wisconsin offenders subject to probation. Utilizing an instrumental variable approach, we estimate that, compared to unmandated treatments, mental health treatments linked to increased court appearances result in a 13 percent higher probability of an offender returning to the justice system within a year due to a new criminal offense. This adverse outcome is primarily observed in cases involving property crimes.

A prevalent challenge in medical image segmentation tasks is the time-consuming and costly process of annotating images at the pixel level. To mitigate this problem, this paper presents a novel deep learning framework called Mask-Aware Attention Network (MAAN), which focuses on effective lung nodule detection and characterization from CT scans using readily available inter-slice annotations. The MAAN achieves this by reconstructing pixel masks through a hierarchical strategy that leverages a coarse-to-fine approach, combining multiple instance attention mechanisms and a series of instance-aware refinement modules. Notably, the MAAN can be easily adapted to various segmentation tasks by simply reusing its basic components. Extensive experiments conducted on two public lung nodule datasets demonstrate the MAAN's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods when only nodule masks are available for training, and highlight its potential as a practical solution for improving lung nodule detection and characterization when pixel-level annotations are scarce.

The performance and lifespan of materials are significantly impacted by local atomic disorder, a key factor influencing various material properties. Understanding and predicting these influences at an atomic level is essential. Traditional methods for analyzing diffraction data, such as pair distribution functions, provide an average view of real-space structure but fail to capture the variability present in most materials. This variability is often associated with localized structural defects, a critical factor affecting the behavior of materials. We introduce a methodology for decomposing experimental or simulated scattering data into distinct real-space components, categorized by their structural integrity. This approach, called the Complete Distribution Functions (CDF), enables the analysis of disorder from scattering data, offering a comprehensive view of real-space structure. We demonstrate the utility of CDF by conducting a comprehensive study on the structural characteristics of metallic glass formed through rapid cooling, utilizing X-ray diffraction data. Our findings reveal that this material is composed of a wide range of structural components, including highly ordered crystals, moderately ordered nanoclusters, and highly disordered regions, all coexisting within the glass. As the material transitions from its liquid state to a glassy solid, specific regions become increasingly stable, eventually forming the building blocks of the glass. This method not only uncovers previously unknown aspects of metallic glass formation but also offers a robust framework for analyzing and interpreting structural dynamics across various materials.

Consider a scenario where the probability of an event, such as a claim, is not uniform but follows a distribution among a group of individuals, and independent and identically distributed probabilities within each subgroup give rise to a compound distribution. This concept is highly relevant to fields like risk theory and epidemiology. This paper investigates Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators for various estimation methods, including Kullback's, NPS, and empirical Bayes, by formulating their objectives as optimisation problems. By doing so, it leads to novel likelihood functions and allows for the use of standard statistical software. The proposed estimators' performance is evaluated through a simulation study, comparing their results to Maximum Likelihood Estimators and Bayesian methods, particularly focusing on their distribution outputs, biases, and root mean squared errors.

Knowledge tracing has seen a significant rise in the use of deep learning models, yet these models often struggle with the issue of overfitting due to their high capacity. This paper presents a new deep learning model, named ETT, which utilizes an attention-based autoencoder to tackle the problem of overfitting in knowledge tracing. ETT is designed with two key components: an encoder that combines multiple autoencoders to capture different patterns in student data, and a predictor that leverages the differences between these encoders. Additionally, a predictor mask is introduced to select relevant autoencoder features. A contrastive loss function is then employed to optimize the model's parameters. A significant portion of the paper is dedicated to explaining ETT's architecture, as well as discussing various baselines and auxiliary methods. A range of public datasets is used to evaluate the proposed method's effectiveness. A case study further illustrates a predictor's ability to capture distinct patterns in student performance. A visual analysis of the model's attention mechanism is also conducted to gain deeper insights. A final discussion section offers suggestions for future research. A supplementary section provides further details on baseline methods, a step-by-step explanation of ETT, and additional experimental results.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's proof format debuted,  
which has since seen significant improvement through the efforts of various teams.  
Given the format's popularity among research groups seeking to build upon high-quality proof techniques,  
it is now crucial to safeguard against unintended modifications.  
To address this need, we have created veriT-proof 10.0,  
a stable, unchanging version of the proof format that will remain unaffected  
by future developments in veriT.

As the number of mobile devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, it significantly hampers training efficiency. This issue becomes even more pronounced when dealing with a vast number of contributors, as seen in large-scale projects like Google's NGC. To address this challenge, we present an innovative algorithm, NGC-AGG, which leverages the benefits of batch processing while maintaining the agility needed for systems with a vast number of active participants. Our research shows that NGC-AGG, our proposed algorithm, can achieve significant speedups, as evidenced by experiments on NGC testbeds with over 100,000 devices and production-scale projects.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition (ASR) has seen a significant boost in performance due to the use of external knowledge. While some research has explored expanding the alphabet to aid ASR, its application in clean environments is limited. In noisy conditions, however, this method has shown substantial improvement. In this work, we explore a more strategic way to expand the alphabet by only including phonemes that are highly distinguishable, and we achieve this through an attention-based selection process during the training phase. In this modified model, the ASR is trained without labels for selected phonemes, and we compare our approach to one with all phonemes and two clean baselines. In this study, we focus on two datasets, and to test the robustness of our method, we explore various noise conditions. Our results show that this phoneme-selection approach notably enhances performance in various noise environments but has a marginal effect in clean conditions.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots face when navigating complex, time-sensitive underwater settings by simultaneously managing multiple navigation objectives and accounting for sensor inaccuracies.  By integrating Gaussian Process regression into the TD learning framework, our method enhances NP estimates by leveraging precise temporal information and reduces noise in pressure readings through careful selection of a reproduction kernel and precision matrix.  Through simulated and real-world experiments, our proposed method demonstrates superior performance in terms of navigation accuracy and efficiency when compared to traditional TD learning and Gaussian Process regression-based TD learning approaches that neglect temporal dynamics or require manual noise estimation.

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant approach to describe a static and spherically symmetric star, free from symmetry reduction, and derive the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in this framework. Next, we analyze energy conditions, causal sound speed, and the influence of spacetime curvature on these conditions. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of mass and pressure on the star's structure, as well as the conditions for hydrostatic and adiabatic stability. Finally, we confirm energy conservation and verify that the star remains visible in this model.

Most current GEC methods focus on improving model parameters using annotated data, but real GEC challenges often involve domain shifts without annotated target data. This paper reexamines the problem and presents a new framework for a few-shot domain adaptation that leverages language decoders. We propose training language decoders to produce accurate translations of incorrect sentences, treating GEC as a sequence-to-sequence prediction task. However, this approach is computationally intensive for multiple domains. To address this, we introduce a meta-learning framework that trains decision makers to control the GEC model and produce controlled outputs. Experiments on the ISLE dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our meta-learning approach, outperforming strong baselines in a few-shot setting without retraining the underlying GEC model. This is achieved with a 0.14 F-score improvement over a baseline that trains language decoders directly, and only a 0.07 lower score than retraining the GEC model for each domain.

The task of allocating goods fairly among self-interested agents, where the number of items and their characteristics are privately known, is a complex problem. While previous research has focused on approximation methods for welfare, an exact solution is possible when there are sufficient items to ensure that each agent can achieve their second-highest possible utility, regardless of the items' values. Although this solution is equitable, it leaves some items unallocated and items may not be valued positively. When items are desirable, a more suitable fairness criterion is needed. This solution can be adapted to allocate items that satisfy EF1, a fairness standard where each agent believes they receive at least as much value as any other agent, when comparing to their most valuable item. This solution is not only fair but also strategy-proof and welfare-maximizing.

UGC 8839, an extremely faint spiral galaxy, has a highly active star-forming region located approximately three kiloparsecs from its nucleus. This unusual characteristic is surprising for such low surface brightness galaxies, which typically have very little gas in their outer regions. To better understand the star formation in UGC 8839, observations were made of its molecular gas using CO emission lines, covering a wide range from -1.5 to +3.0 kiloparsecs. These observations revealed that the extensive star formation in UGC 8839 corresponds to an extended disk of molecular gas, with an average rotation curve that remains flat over the observed distance range. Additionally, there is evidence of two giant molecular clouds rotating in opposite directions, possibly caused by an interaction with a nearby spiral galaxy. To further investigate the cause of UGC 8839's star formation, deep optical imaging was performed, but no significant disturbances were detected, unlike in other similar galaxies where mergers or gravitational tidal forces have been observed to induce star formation. Therefore, UGC 8839 presents a unique case of extensive star formation in a spiral galaxy with low surface brightness, induced by possibly rotating molecular gas disks and galaxy interactions, without any signs of gravitational disturbances.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all combinatorially significant contributions in the correlation time domain.  However, both linear and quadratic terms in the pion's displacement exhibit significant noise levels, particularly towards later times and quark masses far from the physical state.  A switch to hadron helicity basis quark currents significantly reduces correlation functions' intrinsically complex structure but at the cost of a substantial increase in statistical noise, especially for heavier quark masses.  This research's results provide precise lattice QCD correlation time ranges for various quark current combinations and quark masses, enabling more precise extraction of the pion's wave function from the lattice and more accurate correlation length time estimates from hadron helicity basis correlations.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution and their associated properties, such as the mass accretion rates that impact planet formation, is crucial. To achieve this, we developed a new method to interpret population studies of young stellar objects, considering the complex interplay of various influences, including the age distribution of star-forming regions, initial conditions, and the evolutionary dynamics of planetary systems. By applying this approach to a comprehensive study of disk structures, we found that existing models of disk evolution, which primarily consider the influence of the Neumann function, are insufficient. Rather, the distribution of protostellar ages, the fraction of systems in different evolutionary stages, and the evolutionary timescale of disk dissipation, all play significant roles. By combining these factors, we can better understand mass accretion rate distributions and better constrain the statistical properties of planetary systems, which have not yet been explored in previous research.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. In offline learning,
these agents can have significantly different performance levels, which may impact
the overall results of their task. This paper investigates how widely scattered
differences in performance levels among the agents, combined with unknown performance
capabilities can confuse other agents and lead to unnecessary relearning. To address
this challenge, we introduce a new problem setting called offline multi-agent
reinforcement learning with heterogeneous agents, and we modify existing single-agent
methods and FIMA to handle this setting. Our modified methods, when applied to our
new problem setting, show a significant impact of performance heterogeneity,
combined with unknown priors, on the accuracy of agents' policies.

Registering megavoltage (MV) images is a crucial step in creating adaptive treatment plans for cancer therapy. Traditional registration techniques rely on intensity-based methods, which are heavily influenced by the distinct characteristics of MV images. To overcome these limitations, a study proposes a novel registration approach using a sequence of compressed sensing (CS) enhanced optical flows (CSEOFs). In this method, a initial two-dimensional electron gate (2D-EGS) registration is performed using a compressed sensing robust canonical correlation analysis (CSRCCC) based approach (RSection-CSEOFs). This involves applying the CSRCCC to control points to capture shared information between kilovoltage (kV) and MV images, while CSEOFs incorporate is it true that only healthy tissue is affected by changes in intensity. A 2D active contour model (ACM) then refines the registration by incorporating anatomical information from images and treatment plans. Subsequently, a 3D version of the CSEOFs method (3D-CSEOFs) is applied to refine the registration. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed CSEOFs framework in accurately registering rectal cancer patients' MV images with a significant reduction in target volume coverage and dose gradient errors.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay Conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment, highlighting the possibility of instantaneous far-reach effects in quantum mechanics.  This paper revisits Einstein's experiment and employs both the Copenhagen and Many-Worlds interpretations of quantum mechanics to demonstrate that such effects are impossible under both frameworks.  Through a series of local measurements on a distant system's entangled particles, we can determine which state a specific system is in at any given moment.  Consequently, when this system undergoes its own local measurement, it yields an outcome that defies randomness, thereby implying the capacity for local events to influence distant outcomes instantaneously.  However, this contradicts the principle of no superluminal causality, confirming that Einstein's vision of a "God playing dice" scenario is unfeasible under both the Copenhagen and Many-Worlds interpretations of quantum mechanics.

The integration of artificial intelligence and Internet of Vehicles technology has led to an increased reliance on vehicle data, raising concerns regarding privacy and security. As valuable data is collected from vehicles, there is a risk of misuse by service providers, leading to unethical behavior. To address this issue, we explore the potential of using Federated Learning in this context. However, FL has limitations when applied to vehicles, particularly due to communication constraints. In response, we investigate the use of model compression in FL for IoT vehicles. To achieve this, we focus on using sign-only transmission in FL and evaluate various sign-based model compression techniques. We compare these methods and identify the most effective FL framework for IoT vehicles. Additionally, we analyze the results to provide insights into using sign-only transmission FL in a real-world scenario.

V392 Persei, classified as a classical nova, experienced an exceptionally prolonged dimming period that exceeded expectations. Utilizing data from multiple sources, including the ZTF, Pan-STARRS1, and the Gaia mission, researchers compiled comprehensive light curves across various wavelengths, spanning from 3600 to 9000 Angstroms. As the nova's brightness diminished, observations revealed significant emission features, such as doubly ionized oxygen and helium I, by 140 days post-eruption. The majority of the observed spectrum's continuum could be attributed to the thermal radiation from the white dwarf's surface. The nova's decline phase exhibited two distinct phases, with the initial phase lasting over 100 days, an unusually extended duration compared to similar novae. The exceptional longevity of the nova's brightness decline was further highlighted by the presence of a strong, slow-rotating, and highly inclined magnetic field of 10 megagauss within the system's white dwarf.

A proposed precoder and codebook design method leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to create codebooks that enhance downlink communication efficiency. Initially, we develop a precoder and codebook based on channel state information (CSI) feedback from users, then establish a benchmark for comparison. Following this, we apply the K-means algorithm to establish a benchmark for the codebook, subsequently improving it through retraining using existing data. The GMM-based model is then employed to establish a benchmark for the proposed precoder and codebook design method, which is shown to outperform it in terms of communication performance.

A type of dynamic current known as two-dimensional robust crosscurrents perpendicularly flowing through a square lattice structure can persist in a third dimension. We are examining these currents by studying a three-dimensional optical circuit composed of laser-cooled atoms arranged in a square plane and extending through a third dimension. We demonstrate that these currents can be measured using site-resolved imaging techniques. A two-dimensional version of this system can be made robust against defects using a magnetic field, and this method can also be applied to the three-dimensional version. A theoretical model has been developed to explain these findings, and it is explained why cdc stability can exist without disorder using simulation data.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific conditions to be consistent with general relativity. In particular, it is required that the rate of mass change with respect to a null direction does not exceed a threshold, which is equivalent to Dyson's maximum luminosity. In this article, we establish an inequality similar to this condition but in a different coordinate system, specifically the Bondar gauge, for the rate of mass change. We also derive an integral inequality related to this condition, which allows us to determine the minimum distance at which a star of given mass can exist. Furthermore, we discuss an extension of this inequality to a more complex scenario, which could potentially be viewed as a generalization of the theorem relating to the maximum luminosity.

This research paper examines a dual-hop OFDM system with multiple parallel sub-channels, where the first hop uses a fixed power allocation method, and the second hop is wiretapped by an eavesdropper listening on selected sub-channels. The primary objective is to determine optimal power allocation for the second hop to maximize the end-to-end physical layer security, subject to maximum power consumption limits for both power allocation schemes. Due to varying rates across sub-channels in the second hop, various water-filling strategies are considered, and their effectiveness is evaluated. To make the problem more manageable, it is reformulated as a finite variable optimization problem with linear constraints and an objective function, and solved using CVX.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games is their lack of diversity in problem sets, which can lead to biased models and poor generalization.
To address this issue, we present TextAdventures, a dynamic, infinite set of well-structured mystery stories generated by a custom framework called GAMI, which combines human input and artificial intelligence.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of GAMI by evaluating ten different agents on the texts it creates, resulting in significant improvements in task completion rates compared to using pre-generated problems.
Additionally, we release the GAMI framework for use by the research community to further develop text-based games.

Recent LSTM architecture innovations have significantly enhanced their accuracy in various applications. However, these improvements have come at a cost of increased model size. In contrast, this paper focuses on more efficient designs that maintain low latency even when compared to standard LSTM models. To achieve greater efficiency, we develop two novel architectures - ResLSTM and VaResLSTM - which incorporate channel reshaping, convolutional layers, and residual connections. These techniques allow for significant reductions in the number of parameters and operations required, while maintaining a level of accuracy comparable to highly regarded LSTM models, such as the VaFormer and the Attention LSTM. Notably, the VaResLSTM model incorporates all components of the VaFormer and can achieve comparable results with substantially fewer parameters and operations required. To test our models, we apply them to multiple forecasting problems across different domains, including electricity consumption, air pollution, and stock prices. These experiments yield promising outcomes, demonstrating that the VaResLSTM model can produce outstanding performance with enhanced computational efficiency. The source code for our models is available on GitHub.

The rapid expansion of wind and solar power generation necessitates more flexible backup generation, drawing from various sources including gas turbines, hydroelectric power, and demand response. To effectively allocate these resources, electricity markets must be restructured. However, the efficiency of existing electricity markets, such as the Norwegian one, is in doubt due to large orders in the secondary redispatch markets, which can be exacerbated by participation strategies that may not be optimal. This study presents a new modeling approach for these markets, which accounts for both continuous and discrete elements, and develops a stochastic bi-level model to evaluate the redispatch market, considering risk and robust optimization. Applying this model to the Norwegian market reveals that using large orders in the redispatch markets is potentially exploitable, which could be used to manipulate the market for personal gain. This behavior is particularly evident when risk and robust optimization are considered. As a result, it is concluded that order breaking strategies employed by market participants are suboptimal and may be manipulating the market.

R.W.K. Odoni established in 1984 that the Galois group of the $n$-th composed version of a generic monic polynomial of degree not equal to zero, $\Theta \in \mathbb{K}[T]$ with coefficients in a field of characteristic zero $\mathbb{K}$, is the symmetric group $S_{d^n}$, where $d$ is the degree of $\Theta$. This result is composed with itself $n$ times and is fully iterated. If the field $\mathbb{K}$ has characteristic greater than zero, the Galois group is the semi-direct product of the symmetric group $S_d$ with a triangular group of monomial matrices, under specific conditions.

Saturn's polar atmosphere has experienced persistent warm areas since 2010, which are associated with broad warm swirls in the stratosphere at 0.5 to 0.4 times the 1-mbar pressure level in both north and south poles. These features are linked to planetary wave activity and temperature patterns with westward-moving meanders, which are also seen in the upper atmosphere of Earth and the lower atmosphere of Jupiter. To better understand the connection between wave activity and temperature patterns in Saturn's polar atmosphere, scientists used Cassini's UV spectrometer to map the 1-mbar pressure level's temperature distribution in the north polar stratosphere between 2010 and 2017, which revealed the formation of broad warm vortices and associated zonal winds in the 0-60 degree latitude range. Based on data from the upper atmosphere of Earth, Jupiter, and Saturn, these features are caused by 5,1000-wavenumber planetary waves that are reflected by strong eastward jets and block the jet's further intensification. Earlier studies have shown that these waves can be triggered by convection and cloud-top instabilities, which are common in Saturn's 90-degree north polar atmosphere.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of mass-supercritical focusing nonlinearity, denoted as $|u|^{p}u$, in a space where the mass lies between $d$ and $d+2$ dimensions. We demonstrate that solutions in this context break down in a finite time, and we do so by deriving a universal upper bound for their rate of growth. Moreover, we establish that the rate of growth is bounded from above by a specific exponential function of a polynomial in time, and we do so by utilizing a new inequality that we also introduce. This inequality, which we call the sharp Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality at the threshold of sobolev regularity, provides a universal upper limit for the gradient of solutions. We also show that these results can be generalized to nonlinearities exhibiting a three-parameter invariance and displaying polynomial scattering behavior at infinity.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearisation functor, resulting in a subcategory of k-fold vector bundles. These vector bundles are equipped with symmetric morphisms associated with the symmetric group Sn. A significant observation arises in the degree 2 scenario, where this added structure leads to the concept of symplectic double vector bundles. These have an opposite relationship with metric double vector bundles. The process of full linearisation is also used to extend N-manifolds and a supermanifold's normal bundle through a linearity functor.

This informal note begins by outlining the fundamentals of algebraic tori, then explores their relationship to orbital integrals and sine functions before concluding with a summary of Tamagawa numbers and their applications.

The interaction between light and matter is central to various spectroscopic methods, where precise measurements of how light matters are critical. A new technique, known as ultrafast coherent Raman scattering, has been used to gain insights into molecular dynamics following light interaction. This work combines a theoretical model with experimental data to investigate the phase information in coherent Raman signals. By analyzing the relationship between an excited molecular state and a scattered photon, we found that the phase in these signals is determined by the energy of a specific molecular vibration, with a distinct feature indicating an exceptionally stable part of the molecular spectrum.

We introduce a novel double-porosity-conductivity model that incorporates two distinct types of fractures within a fractured porous medium: highly conductive fractures and less conductive microcracks between matrix blocks. The former are neglected in most existing models, as they exhibit different transport dynamics compared to Darcy flow, while the latter are commonly described by reduced Darcy flow. The conductive and blocking fractures are respectively modeled with a Reynolds-Osborne flow and a Darcy flow. The model's parameters and structure are validated through a laboratory experiment measuring fluid flow in a porous medium with varying levels of fracture conductivity. The resulting model equations are then confirmed by the experimental data.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in scientific discovery across various disciplines. In this domain, Bayes factors serve as a key tool for comparing competing hypotheses. Despite their usefulness, researchers have historically struggled to understand how Bayes factors should be applied in a meaningful way. In contrast, probabilistic programming has facilitated the widespread adoption of Bayes factors in statistical modeling. In this work, we leverage pp-ppp, an extension of the probabilistic programming framework pp, to systematically explore how hypothesis comparison via Bayes factors is implemented in such software. By examining the theoretical underpinnings of Bayes factors within the context of pp, we develop a set of criteria to evaluate existing implementations. In this investigation, popular Bayes factor libraries in R and Python are analyzed in order to better understand their underlying assumptions and limitations. In addition, we discuss how these implementations compare in relation to the established literature on Bayes factors.

Discourse indicators, such as 'by contrast' and 'consequently', facilitate the identification of connections between sentences, yet their impact on sentence representation has been inadequately studied. We investigate four hypotheses regarding DLRs' influence on representation: DLRs can be disregarded, they help in learning the meaning of subsequent sentences, they modify the representation of the preceding sentence, and they modify the representation of the following sentence. We conducted experiments using a variety of NLP tasks, including coreference resolution, entailment, and a custom benchmark, to determine which hypothesis is most accurate. Our findings suggest that DLRs modify the representation of the following sentence, under specific conditions, in multiple languages, including English, German, and Spanish.

We investigate a fundamental landscape of a specific type of matrix optimization problem under the given condition that the objective function is invariant to a particular mathematical transformation. Focusing on a widely used factorization method under Riemannian quotient geometry, we analyze a Riemannian landscape of a general objective function that remains unchanged under a unitary transformation. When considering problem-specific cases such as low-rank covariance estimation and semi-definite programming, we find that all stationary points, whether critical points or saddle points, can be easily identified and categorized. When paired with perturbation theory and eigenvalue gap properties, we establish the asymptotic completeness of stationary points, both finite and infinite, and derive the asymptotic behavior of both finite and infinite saddle points. Furthermore, an algorithmic implication of our results is that gradient descent with any step size will not be trapped in finite saddle points and is likely to find a solution that meets the optimal conditions.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms to integrate a variety of social-learning methods into a continuous-game framework, utilizing the BART simulation platform. Our primary objective was to assess the impact of these algorithms on Nash Equilibrium convergence when applied by players. Through extensive computational experiments, we discovered that player populations utilizing certain social-learning strategies reached a Nash Equilibrium state more rapidly than when applying individual learning approaches. Furthermore, our results showed that the emergence of a population-wide Nash Equilibrium was not inevitable, as some social-learning algorithms led to outcomes divergent from the set of Nash Equilibria.

We have identified a condition derived from $d_D\left(\left(I(D))^{(2)}\right)\right)$ and $d_D\left((I(D))^2\right))$ that ensures the symbolic and ordinary power sequences of $I(D)$ will have the same difference in degree for a particular degree, which is related to the sum of the symbolic and ordinary power sequences' differences in degree for a particular degree, as well as the sum of the directed cycle lengths in $D$.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are integral to various safety-critical applications, such as autonomous vehicles, and require a high level of reliability. Despite this necessity, CNN predictions can be prone to significant errors, and current error-correction methods often fail to consider the constraints of physical laws. In a critical finding, we demonstrate that simple, computationally inexpensive adjustments can substantially enhance the stability of a CNN's responses and prevent errors that could have catastrophic consequences. Specifically, we show that applying basic magnitude constraints to a CNN's activation levels in its intermediate layers can yield a more reliable and physically consistent set of outputs, with no negative impact on the network's computational efficiency. Our research also reveals that moderate activation clipping results in a more robust set of outputs, exhibits a lower degree of out-of-distribution predictions, and produces a more accurate and less biased sets of predictions in medical diagnosis tasks. In summary, our findings indicate that activation clipping in the CNN's feedforward process can significantly improve the network's reliability without compromising its computational efficiency.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version known as the generalized Jordanian twist. This generalized version satisfies the necessary algebraic conditions and can be used to modify a universal enveloping algebra. Furthermore, we have identified a specific type of quantum deformation of coboundary algebras called quantum $z$-beta constant algebras. These algebras result from applying the generalized Jordanian twist to certain commutative algebras. This research has significant implications for constructing quantum invariant functionals on closed oriented surfaces.

popular Word Sense Disambiguation task. Our approach extends existing techniques 
by incorporating language-specific knowledge through a shared understanding of 
words across different languages. We extract three key elements for clustering 
the senses of words: their meanings in each language, their general meanings 
unaffected by language, and their language-specific characteristics. We 
incorporate specific knowledge into our model using a neural network 
architecture. Our results on four language-specific tasks in the SemEval 2022 
competition show our method's effectiveness, with our team achieving a strong 
performance and a top-three ranking in the overall disambiguation track.

The initial production of particles in high-energy collisions is strongly influenced by the overall number of created particles. A pattern observed in data from various collision types indicates the development of collective radial flow at the end of these reactions. A theoretical explanation for this observation relies on an increased interaction between particles in more complex, highly occupied systems with quark-like properties. As a result, the initial momentum distributions of produced particles exhibit minimal flow effects and match the universal parametric connection between radial flow and particle number seen in observations.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances swept through central Chile, particularly in Santiago. To better understand the spatial spread of these riots, researchers utilized public transportation data and news reports to create detailed maps of rioting activity. By analyzing the connection between initial sparks and the subsequent expansion of unrest, they found that local demographics, transportation networks, and even weather conditions played a role in shaping the events' geography. Notably, temperature alone was insufficient to explain the disturbances' spread, and while public transportation played a role, its impact was limited. Ultimately, this study's findings can inform predictive models for future riots and have implications for policy-making.

Quantum mechanics relies on operator algebra, where raising and lowering
frequently results in non-integer "higher" or "form" versions. Although initially
hypothesized, these variants have recently been confirmed experimentally across
various fields. Here, we theoretically establish a new "higher" variant of a well-known
wirelike Weyl semimetal model. This new model exhibits an unusual "sharper"
cornerlike Weyl semimetallic behavior, which changes into a highly symmetric
fwhirl semimetallic state upon applying a perpendicular magnetic field.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on measurements taken within a domain, where the surrounding space is unbounded. To solve this issue, we employ a hybrid approach combining quasi-reversibility method with boundary integral equations. First, we extend the available measurements into the surrounding space using a layer potential quasi-reversibility method. Next, we derive the missing information on the object's boundary by applying the Chernov formula, and finally we acquire the extended target by sampling along rays within the space. We establish the stability of this method and demonstrate its stability in discrete form after using a conforming edge finite element approach. Through multiple examples, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method.

This research introduces an innovative approach, Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA), for optimizing model training in federated learning by engaging only a subset of participants. FedSA leverages a non-negative scoring system to assess the contribution of each participant's model updates, updating these scores based on a modified Reinforcement Learning (RL) method. As an innovative step, we developed a customized policy gradient algorithm that integrates the performance of two prominent policies, resulting in efficient model training with reduced memory usage. Experimental evaluations across multiple benchmark datasets, including NIST, Show, and Wiki, along with large language models like BERT and LongAct, demonstrate the FedSA approach consistently surpassing state-of-the-art methods in terms of model performance.

We examine how elliptic curves defined within the rational numbers change when subjected to quartic extensions of the rational numbers, specifically those with Galois groups isomorphic to S4 or A4, and we investigate the connection between their ranks in these extensions. Building on a method by Dharmavelan and Poonen, we develop the framework to analyze these changes, and we demonstrate how the rank in $K$ can be represented as the sum of the rank in rational numbers, an even rank component, and a component with a specific parity, where this final component can vary independently, and we show how its range can be expanded from a previously established result.

A fundamental inequality in physics, the quantum null energy condition (QNEC), limits the relationship between null directions, energy-momentum tensors. This paper investigates the null directions along which a free scalar field theory's entropy changes, particularly when considering massless variants. By proving a lower bound that mirrors the QNEC, we establish a connection to an inequality governing inequalities derived by Hollands and Wald. This connection holds true not only for conformal field theories but also for massive field theories. This finding is supported by explicit calculations and numerical evidence. This discovery is backed by both direct computation and numerical support.

We investigate the minimum time required to distinguish two qubit states evolving through unitary transformations given a constraint on evolution speed. We establish that this time can be determined by a unit-invariant measure of state distinguishability known as asymmetry monotones. We specifically analyze the impact of angular distances and their corresponding asymmetry monotones, showing that they provide the most efficient way to distinguish slow-evolving qubit states when viewed through rotation. We further extend these findings to broader classes of qubit states and operator spaces, and explore their relevance to Heisenberg time scales in the presence of strong interactions.

Consider a unit cube in n-dimensional space, denoted as $Q_n$, and let $C(Q_n)$ represent the set of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to the real numbers. The norm for a function in this space is given as the supremum of the absolute values of the function over $Q_n$. A family of subdomains in space is called regular if the infimum of the ratios of the sum of side lengths to the norm of their characteristic function is greater than zero. A family of grids in space is considered quasi-uniform if it is uniform in each of its dimensional components. This paper proves that both the family of difference cylinders and difference spheres in space are quasi-uniform, and as a result, difference schemes with these grid families have stable norms and a set of functions with a specific property that is crucial for the analysis of certain numerical methods.

Superconducting quantum circuits are advancing rapidly as a leading platform for quantum computing. These systems will soon require error mitigation techniques at the hardware level to address material flaws that cannot be corrected by quantum code. This study demonstrates that a two-level system within a superconducting qubit can reach a long-lived, fault-tolerant state without using laser-like resonance. By fully characterizing the material defects in the qubit environment and identifying their specific interactions, the authors found that an engineered energy alignment with certain defect states can induce a stable state for the qubit. This state, located between the qubit's energy levels and immune to external noise, corresponds to a particularly deep and long-lasting qubit operation. The record duration of this state, observed in a qubit circuit, amounts to over a million clock cycles and exceeds previous achievements by an order of magnitude.

This work employs a comprehensive volcanic model, coupled with detailed atmospheric and surface evolution equations, to examine the complex interplay between volcanism, greenhouse gases, and liquid water on early Earth-like planets. We investigate how massive volcanic eruptions can either trigger a runaway greenhouse effect or excessive cooling and water loss, depending on a planet's atmospheric and oceanic conditions. Our model reveals that the feedback loop between water vapor, volcanism, and liquid water creates oscillating periods of warming and cooling, with potential implications for a planet's habitability. Our model is applied to early Earth, Proxima b, and 51 Peg, demonstrating its versatility across different planetary systems.

Point processes, which capture timestamps and characteristics of specific types of events, are extensively utilized in various fields, including financial analysis, telecommunications, and epidemiology. In this paper, we investigate a particular type of event data known as event-type Hawkes processes, which are self-exciting and capable of modeling excitation and inhibition between events of different types. In particular, we focus on linear models, but also briefly explore implications for nonlinear models. We provide an in-depth review of existing literature, Annotated with links to open-source implementations. Additionally, the statistical properties of these processes are examined in greater detail.

We have developed a concept for an ultrafast plasma waveplate that leverages the modification of a Bose-Einstein condensate of $^{87}$Rb atoms through femtosecond laser pulses to precisely control the plasma density pattern. This innovation enables a density grating that acts as a diffraction element, facilitating the conversion of circularly polarized light to linearly polarized light. Despite being mediated by a plasma mechanism, this transformation achieves near-complete efficiency, transforming 100-femtosecond pulses of 795-nanometer light with minimal temperature dependence. The delay between the optical excitation and polarization change can be accurately adjusted from 0 to 9-nanoseconds, providing an extremely precise tool to study both fast timescales and long-term processes in a relativistic atom system. The high density and speed of this plasma platform make it an optimal tool to investigate various processes, including Raman sideband cooling, and provide a valuable extension of recent experiments on FC-ABC cycles using ultrafast plasma density patterns.

Re-examining the search for a non-zero electric dipole moment in the tau lepton, denoted as $d_\tau$, involves considering its connection to lepton flavour violation and CP violation. This study takes into account sophisticated hadronic effects and incorporates information from $B$-meson decays, specifically $B^0\to \tau^+\tau^-\ X^0_{CP}$, where $X^0_{CP}$ represents a CP eigenstate found in $B$-meson decays. Focusing on the decay $B^0\to K^{*0}\tau^+\tau^-$, we analyse the impact of such effects on the electric and magnetic form factors of the tau lepton, which are relevant for $B^0\to K^{*0}\tau^+\tau^-$ decays. Our research reveals that the constraints on $d_\tau$ and its associated form factors can be significantly enhanced, by up to an order of magnitude in some cases, compared to analyses that neglect these effects. For instance, if both tau leptons decay into electrons and hadrons, we anticipate the potential to probe $d_\tau$ down to $4.0\times 10^{-27}\,e\cdot{\rm cm}$ at the High-Luminosity LHC. Additionally, we provide detailed tables of expected sensitivities for various decay modes at both the LHC and a future $e^+

We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main results. Firstly, we show that for codes whose rank distance is greater than one, there exist codes with efficient algorithms to decode any messages subject to a symmetric rank error pattern. These codes can have a large outer code and a comparatively large outer dimension, resulting in a minimum rank distance comparable to that of a Gabidulin code. Moreover, there is a feasible algorithm to decode such codes subject to a symmetric error pattern of low rank. Secondly, we provide a method to decode low-density parity-check (LDPC) rank metric codes with a rank distance equal to two, using a feasible algorithm that can interpret the syndromes and produce coset leaders for the cosets they represent.

Building on previous work by Li and Song, we develop integral representations for OPE block functions corresponding to spinning primary fields through双排列变换. This new formula accurately captures the desired symmetry properties and facilitates direct application in conformal field theory, particularly in computing three-point correlation functions. As a concrete example, we calculate the corresponding fields in $\phi^4$ theory using its free field expansion. Notably, our formula aligns with the results obtained via Feynman diagrams.

In 1994, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local combinatorial structure for complex Pontrjagin classes within rational cohomology. We deepen this understanding by developing a refined combinatorial framework for the entire complex cohomology of Riemannian torus actions on compact Riemannian torus manifolds, specifically those without flat components. As a result of our work, we achieve a complete description of complex cohomology for such manifolds with closed oriented torus actions, and in addition, we establish a complex structure for G-manifolds equipped with isolated torus actions.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo, a bright Type II supernova visible from Earth, during its initial two months as it was observed in SN 1994D, an active region of the Messier 82 galaxy. The supernova resulted from the explosion of a bright blue star in SN 1994D's brightest star and was seen from Earth as an apparent magnitude of 4.5 in U-band. The luminosity of SN~2020jfo is comparable to other bright Type II supernovae, as evidenced by its SN 1993J-like light curve and absolute magnitude of -19. This suggests the supernova was the product of a massive progenitor with a mass between 20 and 30 solar masses. The supernova was also found to be associated with a bright blue transient in SN 1994D, as evidenced by the absence of a significant host galaxy contribution. The analysis of the host galaxy spectrum also revealed the supernova was a core-collapse event that resulted in a highly massive progenitor.

To significantly decrease the number of image sensors needed in wide-field X-ray monitors based on lobster-eye structures, we propose employing multiplexing techniques. By dividing the field of view into multiple lobster-eye sections, each with a distinct directional sensitivity, we can combine their individually monitored sub-fields to create a comprehensive wide-field monitor. For effective implementation, we investigate two digital demultiplexing approaches using scattered X-ray signals in the fish-eye fields of view. The first method utilizes a machine-learning-based classifier to identify the origin of a detected X-ray, whereas the second method leverages the unique directional properties of lobster-eye structures to pinpoint the source of scattered X-rays. We evaluate these demultiplexing techniques through Monte Carlo simulations, assessing their potential for a 20-degree wide-field X-ray monitor composed of multiple lobster-eye sections.

We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations.

To investigate the impact of velocity information on halo formation, we used two high-resolution N-body cosmological simulations, each with $2048^3$ grid points and $2^{18}$ halo masses. The first simulation incorporated standard initial conditions, while the second excluded small-scale fluctuations from the matter power spectrum. We compared the resulting halo populations in both simulations to analyze the influence of halo merging on mass predictions. Our halo finding algorithm, based on an extended hierarchical model, divided halos into retained and merged halos. We found that halo mass from the DHAB code matched halo mass from GADGET2 within 1 percent, indicating the absence of numerical artifacts in our simulation. However, excluding small-scale fluctuations led to a 10 percent increase in $0.2$-percent halo formation at $z=0$. Velocity information was found to be a key factor in halo formation, with halo mass from the PS2 simulation differing by 5 percent from the DHAB code at $z=0$. Retained halos showed a mass difference of 1 percent between the two simulations, while merged halos showed an even more significant difference of 10 percent. Our findings indicate that including halo halo merging in halo models is necessary to accurately predict the halo mass function.

We have developed a novel approach to creating equilibrium configurations of rotating stars within the framework of general relativity. By utilizing a Lagrangian formulation, we have derived a set of differential equations that describe the dynamics of a rotating star in steady state. Furthermore, we have implemented a numerical integration method with boundary conditions at both the center and surface of the star to determine key parameters ensuring physically meaningful solutions. As a result, we have successfully modeled a rotating star in analytical form and computed its structure numerically, applying it to the equation of state introduced by Henyey and Shaw.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for fine-tuning both classification and generation models, which iteratively uses accept/reject outcomes to automatically select model predictions, creating self-supervised training data. Our experiments, conducted using a dataset of nearly 4,000 invoices, demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, which is evaluated using the standard F-score metric, in comparison to various baselines.

The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA detector network has identified signals from merging compact binary systems through three categories: binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole systems. The precise times of these events enable multi-messenger astronomy, combining data from gravitational waves and electromagnetic observations, to locate events in the sky and prompt rapid follow-up observations. The neutron-sterile neutrino event event GW190521, occurring at 8.7 GeV, offers an ideal opportunity to investigate this event through follow-up observations. The LIGO and Virgo collaborations estimate the neutron star remnant event rate to be between 0.09 and 0.83 times the merger rate of definitive neutron star binaries, with 50% of these events potentially hidden within the GW190521 uncertainty range. The neutron-sterile neutrino event event GW190521 could give rise to the neutron-sterile neutrino event event rate, the gamma-ray burst rate, or both, with a small probability of 2%.

Urban environments with high population density drive economic productivity and innovation, yet they also increase disease transmission risks. To analyze this relationship, we developed a novel metric, GeoCon, to quantify spatial interactions in cities. GeoCon combines mobile data from over 100 major global cities to evaluate how population density impacts physical encounters and, consequently, economic growth. Our analysis reveals that the impact of crowding on social interactions is non-linear, with a "Goldilocks zone" where moderate crowding maximizes interactions. This non-linear interaction also affects economic productivity, suggesting that urban planning should consider balancing population density to optimize both social encounters and public health.

Observations from infrared astronomy reveal that high mass young stellar objects display distinctive patterns in their light fluctuations, which may be caused by an unstable flow of material orbiting a central object. This study focuses on creating a theoretical model of nonlinear interactions between gravitational forces and fluid dynamics in a disk, which could potentially replicate observed fluctuations in their infrared emissions. Using a 1D model of an accretion shaft connecting an oscillating disk to a star, we developed and solved equations that account for alternating periods of nothing reaching the star and abrupt increases in accretion rates. These rates were found to be heavily influenced by the material properties of the disk, including density, size, and how quickly it breaks up. Furthermore, we found that the relationship between the intervals of silence and their accompanying bursts follows a power law pattern, which aligns with observations made using the VLTI/GRAVITY instrument. However, to confirm this alignment, more precise measurements are needed, especially as the period of silence extends.

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with Steklov boundary conditions on the free surface. We focus on constant vorticity flows and examine both inviscid and dissipative Stokes flows. Our study explores how these flows cause fluid motion on the surface of water, leading to unique patterns of movement. We analyze two scenarios: when the stronger flow is positioned deeper in the water, and when it is closer to the surface. Our findings reveal that the direction of the flow can either promote or hinder wave movement, depending on the position of the stronger flow. Additionally, we discover that as the flow slows down near the surface, water moves towards it, and that this movement can lead to unique patterns of movement on the surface of the water. Ultimately, this research has implications for understanding how water moves in response to different types of flow, and can help us better predict and manage these movements.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally compact spaces with certain structural properties. To establish this result, topos theory and sheafy differential forms theory are applied to provide an alternative characterization of differential forms. Consequently, the generalization of de Rham cohomology to these spaces is examined.

In complex and unpredictable environments, navigation tasks often require the robot to operate in adverse conditions where typical sensor modalities like LiDAR and cameras may not be reliable, especially in smoky settings. This paper presents a novel approach to indoor navigation for mobile robots that can effectively navigate through smoke-filled rooms using a reinforcement learning-based policy. The policy fuses information from multiple sensors, including a camera, LiDAR, and additional inputs, to navigate in smoky conditions. The proposed method is trained in a realistic simulation where the robot's sensory inputs accurately reflect real-world conditions, accounting for the scattering effects of smoke on camera images. The results show that the policy, which utilizes a multi-sensory input, is capable of successfully navigating through smoke-filled rooms, even when LiDAR sensors are unavailable. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits transferability, allowing it to navigate in clear conditions after being trained solely in smoky conditions.

The prevalence of fake news has been a persistent issue for decades, yet the
2016 US Presidential Election seems to have amplified its impact significantly.
Many individuals have turned to Twitter and other social media platforms as their
primary source of news, inadvertently facilitating the rapid dissemination of
fake stories. To better understand and counter this phenomenon, it is crucial to
identify and analyze genuine as well as fabricated news on platforms like Twitter.
In this work, we present a novel approach to feature extraction that captures the
context in which news is shared on Twitter. Specifically, we investigate various
content-based features, including the semantic content of retweet texts, the
semantic content of user mentions, and the structural properties of the mention
graph, along with platform-specific features such as follower counts and
mention-graph structures like strongly and bipartite components. Through extensive
experiments on two large-scale datasets, our results demonstrate that dynamic,
context-based features derived from mention graphs effectively distinguish
news-related tweets from spam and, when combined with content-based features,
significantly enhance the performance of machine-learning models tasked with
classifying news-related tweets from spam and fabrications. Our approach is
particularly effective in detecting low-efficiency fabrications and provides
valuable insights into the distinct propagation patterns of low-efficiency
fabrications compared to high-efficiency ones.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns, focusing on the geometric properties of systems that behave like Gaussian random fields. We develop a new geometric approach to study these patterns by using the Fisher information matrix as the basis for our geometry. Our developed methodology includes constructing two specialized metrics and studying the resulting geometric properties. We demonstrate the applicability of this approach by analyzing the intricate patterns that emerge from a complex system known as Loève-Stein process. Additionally, we compare the geometry of this pattern to the standard Brownian motion and heat kernel patterns, revealing both similarities and differences in their geometric behaviors.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with outliers, L1-PCA serves as a robust alternative to conventional PCA. Although L1-PCA is a well-established method, its optimization problem is nonconvex and computationally intensive due to the large number of variables involved. To address this challenge, we propose a scalable approximation called Convex-L1-PCA that reformulates L1-PCA by approximating the objective function and identifying a key variance threshold that can be used to threshold the data. This approach not only reduces computational costs but also guarantees a performance bound in terms of final objective values. Moreover, we demonstrate how to further reduce the size of solutions and extract a robust low-rank solution from the initial solution. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data sets show that our method achieves comparable performance to previous methods while being orders of magnitude faster.

Traditionally, structured annotation of text-based or spoken dialog data involved creating simple, handcrafted features based on human-labeled behavior labels. This approach relied on manual annotation that was both time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies. In contrast, this study explores the use of inconsistency-free, state-of-the-art neural language models, specifically BERT, to automatically generate a rich set of attention-based features. This method requires no human labeling and is demonstrated on four distinct dialog tasks, including machine translation, sentiment analysis, and question classification. These results are obtained through end-to-end models with no additional features, indicating that attention-based BERT models already contain structured information necessary for various NLP tasks. Furthermore, this study identifies instances where automatic labels derived from BERT can be manually refined to enhance model performance, particularly in sentiment analysis. This research is conducted using two data sets, including the English SentEval benchmark and the German SemCor dataset.

For mobile robots to navigate in unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective and adaptable mapping system is essential. This system allows the robot to create a global map that provides a high-level overview of the environment, enabling it to plan a path to explore the area efficiently. Effective mapping systems must be capable of producing a map that's both accurate and up-to-date, while also allowing the robot to navigate along a planned path in real-time. This system must also allow for seamless integration of local and global maps, and be able to manage mapping failures by identifying and handling them automatically. In this work, a novel front-end framework is presented that generates a global map, enables navigation along planned paths, and seamlessly integrates and manages various map representations, all in a fully automatic fashion. This framework's capabilities are showcased through simulated experiments and real-world demonstrations.

One of the primary challenges in metrology is accurately measuring very small fractions, such as 1 part in 10^5 to 10^9, of a given physical quantity. This difficulty is compounded by the fact that superconductivity tends to expel magnetic fields, a property that hinders the development of magnetometers with precision better than approximately 10^-5. However, a new method to achieve high-precision magnetic field sensing based on time-domain measurements has been identified, one that is capable of reaching absolute levels of accuracy and relatively easy-to-use standards for absolute measurements with a precision between 10^-6 and 10^-7. This approach, which is also applicable to relative measurements, can be realized by using a superconducting loop that includes a Josephson junction, driven by a Josephson frequency reference and driven by an external magnetic field. By analyzing the resulting voltage waveforms, a means to determine magnetic field levels has been established, either by comparing them to a known standard or by directly examining their characteristics. By performing a series of measurements with varying field strengths and comparing the results, it is possible to establish a precision of around 1 part in 10^6 when using time-domain methods to evaluate magnetic field levels in a range from 10^-6 to 10^-7 per Tesla.

In statistical modeling for complex systems, the task of determining a simple admixture model with distinct components can be challenging due to the varying sizes of these components. This research develops the theoretical basis for data-driven component identification and demonstrates through simulations that under certain conditions, the number of components in the model can be accurately determined using Dirichlet Process Mixtures of Gaussian distributions. Additionally, we explore how exploring the underlying space influences the ability to idenitify components when a Dirichlet Process Mixture is used. Our findings reveal that, in some scenarios, even a minimal amount of components can be properly identified with DPMM, whereas in other cases, an excessive amount of components may result when attempting to identify them.

High-performance computing (HPC) applications often involve multiple data types, making it challenging to optimize them using Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO) techniques.
SMMMO is a broad category of HPC tasks, encompassing scenarios where a single optimization method is used on many different objects, such as images, meshes, and matrices.
However, frequently encountered SMMO benchmarks, like image rendering, consist of diverse objects that may have different properties and require different handling, posing significant challenges in developing efficient deep neural network (DNN) inference compilers.
In contrast to more complex SIMMO benchmarks, we focus on a simpler but significant class of problems where objects differ only in size, such as matrices of varying dimensions in solving systems of linear equations.
To make such SMMO problems suitable for DNN inference, we introduce a new compiler, SiMMI, which optimizes inference for multiple benchmarks, including SMMO problems.
SiMMI achieves this by creating a unified symbolic representation of executable code, a dynamic graph that can be dynamically pruned, and a dynamic memory allocator that supports memory reuse.
As a result, SiMMI can efficiently solve DNN-based simulations of real-world problems, such as linear equation solving, with a single trained model, and can also enable diverse applications to share the same infrastructure, including a unified symbolic representation of executable code, which can be displayed as part of a case study.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities embedded in a superconducting layer. A self-consistent method was employed to account for the interplay between impurities within a type-II superconductor layer, resulting in the calculation of YSR state spectra for various magnetic moments. The research reveals distinct local YSR zero-bias peaks in the spectral density, with significant peak splitting observed in the vortices present in the type-II superconductor layer. Peak splitting behavior is closely linked to the arrangement of vortex lattices and can offer a method to determine the vacuum position of vortex cores. Furthermore, the theory demonstrates that YSR states can mediate an anisotropic exchange interaction that aligns with the RKKY interaction, observable even far from the vortex lattice arrangement. The formed magnetic domains within the YSR states can also give rise to Yu–Kondo–Yu composite states within the vortices. The proposed method to detect Ysr-VuRKY interactions is valuable for exploring novel quantum phenomena and potential applications in quantum computing.
